contract.settlement_definition: For the single-game ladders (KXMLBHR) Yes if the named batter, who must be in the official starting lineup and record at least one plate appearance, hits at least N home runs (1+ or 2+) in the listed game; a scratch, a bench start, a zero-PA starter, or a later-entering substitute (pinch hits excluded) refunds at fair price. The archetype also holds series totals (KXMLBSERIESHR: officially recorded home runs across a championship series including extra innings and inside-the-park home runs) and a postseason walk-off count (KXMLBWALKOFFS), plus a large set of Home Run Derby and All-Star Game series that have only titles.

rules_evidence.quote: If Sal Frelick is not in the starting lineup but later enters the game, the market will resolve to the fair market price, pinch hit at bats will not count towards the market.
rules_evidence.establishes: Single-game HR ladder excludes substitutes and refunds at fair price; population is starters with a PA.

rules_evidence.quote: This market counts the named player's total officially recorded home runs across the entire series, including extra innings and inside-the-park home runs.
rules_evidence.establishes: Series HR total counts all HRs in the series (including extras and inside-the-park) with no start gate, a different object from the single game.

rules_evidence.quote: A walk-off occurs when a game ends with the home team scoring the winning run in the bottom half of the 9th inning or any extra inning.
rules_evidence.establishes: Walk-off count is a team-level game-ending event, not a hitter's HR, and depends on game script in the last inning.

variants_and_edge_cases: Strike construction differs inside the archetype: 1+ and 2+ per game (nested), series 2+ over multiple games, a playoff-wide count of walk-offs with rung 5+, and Home Run Derby markets that have no rules text in the sample (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS).
Inside-the-park and extra-inning home runs count for the series total; for the single-game market the sampled text does not say, but the official scorer count includes them.
Single-game population is conditional on start and one PA; series totals have no such gate, so a hitter who misses a game simply has fewer PAs.
A walk-off HR counts as a home run for the hitter market and as a walk-off for the other; a walk-off can end with a non-HR so the two events are correlated but not identical.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official MLB box score home runs for the player or team; walk-off definition quoted in the rules; presumed MLB Stats API for counts; Derby sources unknown.

mechanism.summary: A home run in a game is the union over the hitter's plate appearances of a low-probability event (about 3 to 6 percent per PA), so P(1+) is approximately 1 minus the product of (1 minus p) over his PAs and P(2+) comes from the tail of a Poisson-binomial. The per-PA probability is a product of hitter power (barrel, pull-air and bat-speed profile), pitcher vulnerability by handedness and pitch type, and a park-weather carry factor that depends on wall geometry in the hitter's spray direction, wind component along that direction, temperature, humidity, altitude and the ball. The number of PAs depends on slot and removal risk, and later PAs face relievers. The event is dominated by Bernoulli luck, so the edge is in the multiplicative environment and matchup terms and in knowing the starter, because HR/FB regresses. Series totals and the playoff walk-off count are aggregations over games with exposure uncertainty (who plays, how many games the series lasts).

stages.name: Participation and PA count
stages.description: The market refunds non-starters and zero-PA starters, so the priced population is starters with at least one PA, and the lineup slot plus game length fix the number of HR opportunities. Because per-PA probability is small, expected HRs are almost linear in PA, so lineup posting and early replacement matter proportionally.
stages.distribution: Binary participation resolved at card time; PA count discrete 3-6.

stages.name: Hitter power profile
stages.description: Per-PA HR probability starts with the batter's batted-ball quality (barrels, exit velocity, launch angle), his pull-air rate (home runs are disproportionately pulled fly balls), bat speed and squared-up rate as early signals, and his HR/FB which regresses toward barrel-implied rate. The profile is hand-specific against pitcher handedness.
stages.distribution: Heavy-tailed hitter heterogeneity: per-PA rates from under 1.5% to over 8% across regular hitters.

stages.name: Pitcher and pitch-type vulnerability
stages.description: The starter's HR/FB, barrels allowed, fly-ball rate and the pitch types he throws in hittable locations determine how much of the hitter's power profile is realised; relievers have different HR vulnerability and handedness. The hitter's pitch-type strengths meet the pitcher's usage in damage zones.
stages.distribution: Pitcher HR vulnerability ranges about 0.6 to 1.8 HR/9; relief HR rates differ and are lower sample.

stages.name: Park, wind and carry
stages.description: The same batted ball is a home run in some parks and a fly out in others: wall distance and height by sector, roof state, wind component along the ball's flight path, air density (temperature, humidity, altitude) and ball characteristics determine carry. Because park factors are averages, deviations by hitter spray profile and day-specific wind matter, and the effect is multiplicative on per-PA probability.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative shift from about 0.6 to 1.6 of the neutral per-PA probability; wind adds game-specific variance.

stages.name: Aggregation, series exposure and counting variants
stages.description: Single-game P(1+) and P(2+) come from the Poisson-binomial over PAs with game-shared environment adding positive correlation across hitters; series totals integrate over number of games and whether the hitter plays each game; the playoff walk-off count is a team-level binomial over games with last-inning script. These are different objects with different exposure drivers.
stages.distribution: Poisson-binomial with overdispersion from shared game environment; series totals are compound over random number of games; walk-off count is a sum of rare events.

opponent_matchup.note: Pitcher HR vulnerability by hand and pitch.

availability_news.note: Scratch refunds, so lineup confirmation is the only news driver.

coaching_scheme.note: Managers do not influence a hitter's HR probability beyond lineup slot and pinch-hitting, both captured in lineup and expected PA; there is no strategic switch (like bunting or intentional walks) that materially changes per-PA HR rate in the sampled contracts.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest and clinched status operate only through whether the hitter starts (lineup card), and per-PA HR probability itself is not documented to change with stakes; the series market's rest effect is within lineup exposure.

officiating_rules.note: The umpire zone and rules shape walk and strikeout rates but not the HR probability per ball in play at the level this contract can price; no rule difference changes whether a ball counts as a home run except inside-the-park, which is rare and counted.

mlb.park_specific_xhr.label: Park-and-weather-specific expected home runs per fly ball (xHR by batted-ball sector)
mlb.park_specific_xhr.mechanism: Whether a hit fly ball clears the wall depends on distance, wall height in that sector, wind component, air density and roof.
mlb.park_specific_xhr.rationale: A park HR factor averages over all sprays; a pull-heavy hitter in a park with a short porch on his pull side gets a very different factor from a spray hitter. Deviation from the average on a specific day (wind out to right) matters most for hitters who hit to that sector.
mlb.park_specific_xhr.measurement: From 4 seasons of batted balls with exit velocity, launch angle and spray angle, fit P(HR | EV, LA, spray) per park by logistic spline with park random effect; add wind component along the spray direction and air density as covariates. For each hitter compute expected HR per fly ball by integrating his empirical (EV, LA, spray) distribution (half-life 200 BIP, shrink to hand-class k = 150 BIP) over the game park with the day's wind and density. Units: probability per batted ball and per PA. As-of: forecast at lineup post.
free_sources: park wall geometry (Ballparks of Baseball / team sites)
raw_data: batted-ball: exit velocity, launch angle, spray, park, HR flag; weather: wind speed and direction, temperature, humidity, pressure; park geometry by sector
mlb.park_specific_xhr.why: Connects hitter spray profile to day-specific carry, a more exact form of the park-by-wind interaction than separate factors.

mlb.relief_hr_vulnerability_by_hand.label: Expected reliever HR vulnerability by hand for the PAs after the starter exits
mlb.relief_hr_vulnerability_by_hand.mechanism: Later PAs face relievers whose HR rate and handedness differ from the starter's.
mlb.relief_hr_vulnerability_by_hand.rationale: HR rates of relievers are not the starter's; relief pitchers are often fastball-heavy but with lower HR/FB, and managers match hands. For a batter with 4 PAs, one or two come against relievers so ignoring them mis-sets the late-PA HR probability.
mlb.relief_hr_vulnerability_by_hand.measurement: Using the starter-exit survival, allocate PA index to likely relievers (top 3-4 by team usage in last 20 games, by hand). Reliever HR rate per PA vs same-hand and opposite-hand batters over 2 seasons half-life 250 BF, shrink to league relief by hand with k = 200 BF. Per-hitter HR probability for PA >= k = hitter power x reliever vulnerability. Units: HR per PA. As-of: bullpen availability at lineup post.
raw_data: PA-level: pitcher id, role (starter/reliever), hand, HR flag, batter hand, inning
mlb.relief_hr_vulnerability_by_hand.why: Team bullpen_talent (xFIP) conflates K/BB with HR; the HR-specific relief exposure is what matters here.

mlb.series_hr_exposure.label: Series home-run exposure: games played distribution x start probability x per-game HR rate
mlb.series_hr_exposure.mechanism: A series HR total is an aggregation over a random number of games in which the hitter may or may not start.
mlb.series_hr_exposure.rationale: The 2+ HR series rung is dominated by how many games the series goes (4-7) and whether the hitter plays each; the per-game HR probability then compounds. Team playoffs and rest days change both exposure and opposing starters (aces vs fifth starter).
mlb.series_hr_exposure.measurement: N_games ~ distribution from series win-prob model (probability each game, length distribution 4-7 for best-of-7); P(start) per game from role (everyday = 0.95, platoon = 0.55 conditional on opposing starter hand); per-game p_HR from the single-game model with each game's probable starter. Series count distribution = compound sum. Units: expected HR in series. As-of: before each game with updated series state.
raw_data: series state, probable starters, games remaining; lineup status per game
mlb.series_hr_exposure.why: Series HR contracts are priced on exposure, not just per-game HR rate.

mlb.game_shared_hr_dispersion.label: Within-game shared HR environment dispersion (wind/ball/pitcher day latent)
mlb.game_shared_hr_dispersion.mechanism: Home runs by different hitters in the same game share environment and pitcher states, so counts are overdispersed relative to independent Bernoullis.
mlb.game_shared_hr_dispersion.rationale: Single-hitter markets need only his marginal, but any multi-hitter or team inference (and the 2+ HR rung) depends on positive dependence; wind blowing out raises everyone's probability together and HR events cluster when a pitcher is lacking command.
mlb.game_shared_hr_dispersion.measurement: From 4 seasons of games compute the variance ratio of team-plus-opponent HR counts to the Poisson-binomial expectation given the matchup model, by park roof type and wind-out strength decile; estimate dispersion phi (negative binomial) shrunk to league with k = 100 games. Units: variance inflation. As-of: through prior games.
raw_data: game-level: HR counts by team, modelled expectation, wind/temperature/park
mlb.game_shared_hr_dispersion.why: Calibrates the 2+ HR rung and joint HR outcomes consistently.

interactions.mechanism: A pull-power hitter's HR probability is the product of his pull-air barrel rate, the park's wall geometry on that side and the wind component along that line; each alone is mild but together they move per-PA probability by factors of two. The spray direction links the hitter profile to the specific wind and wall, so they must be modelled jointly.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate P(HR) per batted ball with a spray x wind x park term and compare with a model using separate park and wind factors.

interactions.mechanism: Per-PA HR probability changes mid-game as the starter is replaced: PAs 1-3 use the starter's vulnerability, PAs 4-5 the reliever's. A homer-prone starter who is pulled early shifts exposure to a different arm, so total HR expectation is a PA-weighted mix conditioned on exit time.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute expected HR with PA-index-specific pitcher vulnerability versus a single starter rate; compare calibration.

interactions.mechanism: Carry gains from thin air and tailwind add to the park norm but saturate near the wall: a ball that clears by feet gains nothing from more carry while a ball at the warning track gains most. The joint effect is therefore concave in the sum of wind and density and strongest for borderline fly balls.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit P(HR) as logistic in distance-over-wall with wind/density shifting the distance; check concavity in wind and density deviations.

interactions.mechanism: HRs of hitters in the same game share weather and pitcher-day factors, so P(2+) and any multi-hitter outcome has positive dependence; the 2+ rung for one hitter is sensitive to the shared factor and to his PA count in the extra-inning tail.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare observed rate of 2+ HR games by hitter strength decile against Poisson-binomial and negative-binomial predictions.

interactions.mechanism: The series 2+ HR rung depends on games played (4 to 7) and start probability per game; because the HR count is convex in exposure (two events needed) the rung probability rises faster than linearly with expected games, and platoon exposure differs by opposing starter handedness.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate series count with different N_games distributions; check sensitivity of P(2+) to series length and platoon start probability.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in barrel rate: HR probability per PA rises faster than linearly with barrel% and pull-air%
nonlinearities.why: HRs concentrate in the top tail of exit velocity and launch angle, so power metrics enter convexly; linear barrel terms underprice elite hitters.

nonlinearities.shape: Asymmetric saturating in wind component: gains from tailwind exceed losses from headwind and both saturate at high speed
nonlinearities.why: Carry depends nonlinearly on speed and wall distance; the same wind has different value for borderline versus deep fly balls.

nonlinearities.shape: Near-linear in PA at small p but with a discrete floor/ceiling at 3 and 6 PA
nonlinearities.why: Per-PA probability is small so 1 - (1-p)^PA is almost linear, but discrete support of PA and extra-inning cases create tails.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating shrinkage with fly-ball count: regression weight falls as ln(FB) rises
nonlinearities.why: HR/FB signal stabilises slowly (hundreds of FBs), so early-season HR/FB should be heavily shrunk and later weights grow slowly.

Extra innings: the automatic runner on second creates additional scoring chances with RBIs for the next hitters, changing the distribution for hitters near the top of the order in the 10th inning.

mechanism.summary: RBIs and stolen bases are both opportunity-conditional counts. An RBI requires runners on base when the hitter bats and an outcome that brings them home under official scoring, so the expected RBIs are a sum over his PAs of the probability of each base-out state times the probability his outcome scores each runner. The base-out state distribution is determined by the hitters ahead (their on-base rates), team scoring and the opposing pitcher, so it is a Markov chain over the lineup. Conversion depends on power, contact and situational outcomes (sacrifice flies, ground balls scoring from third) and excludes double plays. Stolen bases require reaching first (or second), a steal opportunity with the next base open, a decision to go made by runner, manager and game state, and success against the pitcher's time to plate and the catcher's throw. Both outcomes are rare-event counts with zero mass, heavily dependent on lineup slot and the confirmed lineup, and the count distribution is zero-inflated and overdispersed.

stages.name: Lineup gate and neighbours
stages.description: The market refunds non-starters; what matters for the surviving population is the batting slot, who bats ahead (supplying runners) and behind (affecting whether pitchers pitch around him and the stolen-base decision). The lineup card posts late, so ahead-of-him on-base skill is not known until then.
stages.distribution: Binary start gate; neighbour identities change the opportunity distribution materially (a leadoff hitter with a .380 OBP ahead versus a .300 OBP).

stages.name: Runner-on-base opportunity chain
stages.description: Opportunity is the distribution of runners on base when the hitter comes to bat in each of his PAs. It is a Markov chain on the order: the on-base rate of preceding batters, the opposing pitcher's baserunner allowance, and the park run environment determine how often a runner stands on first, second or third (and how many outs), and so how often an RBI is possible at all.
stages.distribution: Discrete base-out state distribution per PA; positive dependence among hitters' states within a game; 40-50% of PAs have no runner on base.

stages.name: RBI conversion given runners
stages.description: Conversion depends on the hitter: power and extra-base rate drive scoring multiple runners, contact and ability to hit fly balls with a runner on third (sacrifice flies), ground-ball tendencies (double plays do not give RBIs) and walk behaviour with the bases loaded. Conversion differs by runner position: a runner on third scores on many outs, a runner on first on few.
stages.distribution: Per-opportunity Bernoulli-like with heavy tail from HR with traffic; correlated with team scoring.

stages.name: Stolen-base attempt and success
stages.description: Stealing needs the hitter on first (or second) with the next base open, then an attempt decision: runner speed and success history, the pitcher's time to the plate and left-handed pickoff, the catcher's pop time and arm, score margin and inning, the manager's green light, and rule changes (bigger bases, pickoff limits) that moved attempt rates. Success then depends on the same battery.
stages.distribution: Rare Bernoulli per opportunity (attempt about 5-10% of first-base opportunities for typical runners, higher for elite); multiple SBs per game possible but rare.

stages.name: Count distribution and ladder nesting
stages.description: RBI and SB counts are zero-inflated and overdispersed relative to a simple Poisson because opportunities cluster in high-scoring innings and one event (a grand slam) can add four; the thresholds 1+ and 2+ for RBI and 1+ for SB are nested events from the same latent opportunity.
stages.distribution: Zero-inflated, right-skewed; RBI heavy tail with clustered runs; SB nearly Bernoulli with small multiple mass.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest and clinched-seed behaviour change RBI and SB totals only by changing who starts and where he bats; no separate schedule driver exists beyond the lineup card, and no stakes effect on a batter's RBI conversion is documented.

officiating_rules.note: RBI scoring rules (no RBI on a GIDP or error) are definitional and covered under settlement; umpire zone has no first-order effect on RBI or SB counts and the 2023 pickoff-limit and base-size rules are handled as the rule regime input.

mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.label: Per-PA base-out state distribution from the confirmed lineup (Markov chain)
mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.mechanism: RBI opportunity is the probability distribution of runners and outs when the hitter bats, derived from the hitters ahead.
mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.rationale: Average RBI opportunity per slot hides lineup-specific variation: the same cleanup hitter has materially more RBI chances behind two .380-OBP hitters than behind two .300-OBP hitters, and opposing starter baserunner allowance scales it.
mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.measurement: Build a nine-state-by-outs Markov chain for the confirmed lineup: transition probabilities per batter (P(1B), P(2B), P(HR), P(BB/HBP), P(K), P(GB DP), P(out other)) from batter true-talent shrunk to league with k = 200 PA and adjusted to the opposing starter and park. Run 10k simulated games or solve analytically to get P(runner on 1B, 2B, 3B; outs) at each of the hitter's PAs; summarise as expected runner-weighted opportunity (sum over runners aboard). Units: expected runners on base per PA. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: PA-level events with base-out state; confirmed lineup and batter splits
mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.why: Exact RBI-opportunity input for the lineup and opponent; avoids averaging slot opportunity over lineups.

mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.label: RBI conversion rate by runner position (1B/2B/3B) and outs, excluding GIDP
mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.mechanism: Given runners, the hitter's chance to drive them in differs by base and outs and includes sacrifice flies, productive outs and HR.
mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.rationale: A batter's RBI per runner on base differs for a power hitter (HR clears everyone) versus a contact hitter (scores runner from third on a fly ball) versus a ground-ball hitter (GIDP, no RBI). Aggregated RBI/PA mixes these roles with opportunity.
mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.measurement: For each hitter over 3 seasons: RBI per runner-on-base-PA split by (3B-only, 2B/3B, 1B-only, bases loaded) x outs (0, 1, 2) from event data; shrink each cell to hand-class cell with k = 40 opportunities. Components: P(HR | state), P(hit | state) and RISP contact rate, P(sac fly | runner 3B, <2 out), P(GIDP | runner 1B, <2 out). Units: expected RBI per PA given state. As-of: through prior game.
raw_data: PA-level: base-out state, outcome, RBI credited, batter, pitcher
mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.why: Separates opportunity from conversion so the model knows why a hitter has RBIs; avoids regressing noisy RISP batting average.

mlb.sb_opportunity_conversion.label: Steal attempt hazard per opportunity (runner on first, second base open) by game state
mlb.sb_opportunity_conversion.mechanism: A steal attempt is a decision at each opportunity influenced by runner, battery, score and rule regime.
mlb.sb_opportunity_conversion.rationale: Season SB totals mix opportunity (how often the runner reaches first) with decision and success; the contract is per game so opportunity is the pivotal driver, and the decision probability depends on score margin (late blowouts suppress steals), pitcher hand and the pickoff-disengagement rule.
mlb.sb_opportunity_conversion.measurement: For each runner over 2 seasons (2023+ rule regime only): attempts / opportunities where opportunity = PA-end or between-PA state with runner on first and second open and fewer than two outs; stratify by pitcher hand (L/R), score margin (|margin|<=3 vs >3) and inning (<=6, >=7). Shrink to speed-class rate with k = 30 opportunities. Multiply by P(opportunity) = P(reach first) from lineup chain and by success probability (runner success rate vs battery pop time + time to plate, shrunk k = 25 attempts). Units: steals per game. As-of: lineup post (catcher and pitcher known).

interactions.mechanism: Steal probability is opportunity times attempt hazard times success; slow pitchers and weak-armed catchers raise both attempt and success for fast runners but have little effect on slow runners, so the battery effect scales with runner speed and manager green light.

interactions.mechanism: The batter behind a runner affects both RBI opportunity and the steal decision: a strong hitter behind a speedster makes managers less likely to send him early, while a weak batter behind raises steal probability. interactions.mechanism: Extra PAs arrive in high-scoring games and the RBI ladder at 2+ needs at least two scoring events, so P(2+ RBI) is convex in the game run environment: low-total games almost never produce 2+ while high-total games do so disproportionately.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in team scoring: 2+ RBI probability rises faster than expected runners on base

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold: attempt hazard jumps above about 28 ft/s sprint speed and saturates near elite
nonlinearities.why: Stolen-base attempts concentrate among the fastest runners; the response to speed is flat below a threshold and steep above.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in combined hold time and pop time: when time to plate plus pop time exceeds roughly 3.3 sec success approaches the runner's maximum

contract.settlement_definition: Mixed family. Single-game spreads (KXMLBSPREAD) pay Yes if the named team wins the listed game by more than the stated run margin (strikes like 5.5), counted on the final score. The head-to-head game winner (KXMLBGAME) and spring-training winner have titles only in the sample, so treatment of extra innings, postponement, suspension and shortened games is not visible. Series winner and series game spread (KXMLBSERIESSPREAD: wins by more than 3.5 games) and division winner (KXMLBALWEST etc.) are also filed here; division winner pays Yes if the team is the 2026 division winner. Source of truth is not named in the sampled text. Only KXMLBGAME's own settlement (extras, shortened, suspended, postponed) remains unverified because it is TITLE_ONLY; claims about it are conditional (see ml_gamewinner_rules).

rules_evidence.quote: If Tampa Bay wins by more than 3.5 games in the Tampa Bay vs Milwaukee Championship Series in the 2026 Pro Baseball Playoffs

Spread strikes are half-runs, so ties after regulation do not matter for the spread; but extra-inning results do (a 1-run walk-off in the 10th gives margin 1), and the margin is of the completed game's final score.

Series spread counts games (3.5 = a sweep in a best-of-7); series winner and series spread depend on the series length process, starters in each game and home-field pattern rather than the single-game win probability.

The ledger also files division winners (AL/NL East, Central, West) and the All-Star Game strikeouts winner in this archetype; these have different mechanisms (season simulation and a one-off exhibition) and are flagged as misfiled.

Series spread object depends on series format: 'wins by more than 3.5 games' is satisfied only by a 4-0 sweep in a best-of-7 (margin 4) and cannot be satisfied in a best-of-5 (max margin 3), so round format is a required contract-level input, not just a game-level one.

mechanism.summary: The winner and run margin of a baseball game come from two teams' run processes that interact only through the pitchers, the park and the weather. Each team's runs are the sum over innings of base-out Markov outcomes: the starter pitches the first five or six innings against a nine-man lineup, then relievers cover the remainder with leverage-driven deployment. Run expectation per half-inning is determined by the starter's run prevention and workload, the lineup's strength against his handedness and arsenal, the defense and catcher behind him, the park and weather, and the umpire's zone. The difference of two overdispersed, inning-clustered counts, with a tie after nine resolved by an automatic-runner extra-inning game, gives win probability and the whole margin distribution. Moneyline is therefore a single cut of a distribution that spread rungs read in the tail: margin strikes depend on how often relief teams hold or extend leads and on blowout variance. The edge is concentrated in market-moving information that arrives late (confirmed lineup, scratched starter, roof and wind), and records must be regressed to run-based talent. Series winners add a game-level dynamic program over announced starters.

stages.name: Who actually pitches and bats
stages.description: Win probability is conditional on the starting pitchers, the nine batters and the catchers who actually play. Probable starters are announced days ahead but change; lineups post a few hours before first pitch and reflect rest days and platoon choices. Before confirmation the market is a mixture over starter and lineup states, so the information structure is a sequence of announcements rather than a single pregame snapshot.
stages.distribution: Discrete mixture over starter identity (small probability of change) and lineup strength (rest-day sits for regulars cut team strength by a few percent of runs).

stages.name: Team run rates by phase
stages.description: Each team's expected runs are split between the starter's innings and the bullpen's innings. The starter's run prevention (SIERA/xFIP/Stuff+) and expected innings set the weight on starter versus bullpen, the lineup's handedness-specific offence faces the starter's arsenal, and defense and catcher framing adjust balls in play and strikeouts. A better-starter advantage equals the quality gap times expected innings, plus the bullpen gap times the remaining innings.
stages.distribution: Expected runs per team around 3.5-5.5 per game with weighting between starter and bullpen that varies by start (innings ranging from 4 to 7).

stages.name: Environment and officiating
stages.description: Park dimensions and altitude scale run scoring for both teams, with handedness-specific effects; wind and temperature shift carry; the roof can change the day's regime; the umpire's called zone changes walk and strikeout rates for both teams. Home-field advantage is more than constant: last-at-bat advantage and park familiarity matter and vary by park.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative factors on run rates (park factor roughly 0.85 to 1.30); home-field edge a few percentage points of win probability.

stages.name: Run-difference distribution and tie resolution
stages.description: The final margin is a difference of two overdispersed, inning-clustered counts; ties after nine innings go to extra innings: the regular season starts each extra half-inning with an automatic runner on second, but to my knowledge (unverified for 2026) postseason games, which the sampled contracts are, start extras with bases empty, so extras resolve with fewer runs per half-inning and the home team's last-at-bat advantage is the walk-off stopping rule. Margin strikes depend on the skew of this distribution and on bullpen deployment: managers use their best relievers in close games and mop-up arms in blowouts, so winning margins are lumpier than a constant-variance model implies.
stages.distribution: Skellam-like with overdispersion and discrete support; sharp mass at one-run margins; extras resolve ties about even with a home edge.

stages.name: Series and division aggregation
stages.description: Series winner and series spread chain single-game win probabilities across a sequence of starters with rest, travel and home-field patterns; division and season markets integrate over the remaining schedule. Postseason series use shortened starter leashes and high-leverage relievers, and game outcomes within a series are dependent through unobserved team strength. This stage is conditional: it describes series/division contracts that the ledger files here but that belong elsewhere (see series_mapping_issues); the series inputs are existing catalog inputs (mlb.series_context, mlb.postseason_leverage_usage, mlb.series_game_state) shared with other archetypes, not defined in this record.
stages.distribution: Dependence through a team-strength latent; series length distribution (4-7 games) is a derived discrete variable.

mlb.lineup_strength_delta.label: Day-specific lineup strength delta (confirmed lineup vs team baseline, in runs per game)
mlb.lineup_strength_delta.mechanism: The nine hitters who actually play differ from the team's season baseline because of rest days, platoon choices and injuries.
mlb.lineup_strength_delta.rationale: Team-level wRC+ averages across the season's lineups; the confirmed card might lack its best hitter or contain a bench bat, and the effect is not uniform across the order (top slots get more PAs).
mlb.lineup_strength_delta.measurement: delta (runs per game) = sum over slots s of PA_share(s) x (wOBA_proj(hitter_s, vs starter hand) - wOBA_proj(team regular at slot s)) / wOBA_scale, with wOBA_scale about 1.2 (so 0.100 team-wide wOBA over about 38 PA is about 3.2 runs); PA_share already sums to about 38.2 PA per game, so no further 9-inning multiplier is applied. Projections from rest-of-season systems (ZiPS/Steamer) blended with 2-season xwOBA shrunk to projection k = 300 PA. PA_share from slot PA expectations (4.65, 4.55, 4.45, 4.35, 4.25, 4.15, 4.05, 3.95, 3.85). Units: runs per game. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: lineup card (hitter, slot), projection table, handedness
mlb.lineup_strength_delta.why: Late lineup news is the main non-market source of game-level edge and has no explicit measured input in the catalog beyond a data feed.

mlb.home_field_run_advantage.label: Park-specific home-field effect (win-probability and run advantage) with last-at-bat component
mlb.home_field_run_advantage.mechanism: Home teams win more often than road teams: last at-bat, familiarity, travel and umpire exposure.
mlb.home_field_run_advantage.rationale: A constant HFA hides park differences (dimensions, sightlines, altitude familiarity) and the structural last-at-bat advantage that produces extra home wins in tied late innings and truncates the bottom-9th when the home team leads.
mlb.home_field_run_advantage.measurement: Estimate team-home (HFA_t) via mixed model on 10 seasons: run margin ~ team strength (home + away) + home indicator + park random effect (shrunk k = 400 games per park) + travel-days indicator; add last-at-bat component = P(home wins | tied entering 9th) - 0.5 from extras data. Output HFA in run margin and win probability for the specific park. As-of: through prior season plus current.
raw_data: game log: home, away, runs, park, date, innings played
mlb.home_field_run_advantage.why: Distinguishes between parks with large and small HFA, and handles walk-off truncation correctly for margin strikes.

mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.label: Reliever deployment by lead size (who pitches innings 7-9 as a function of margin) and its run-prevention effect
mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.mechanism: Managers use high-leverage relievers in close games and low-leverage arms in blowouts, compressing and lumpifying the margin.
mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.rationale: A margin spread cover is not a symmetric diffusion: leads of one to three runs are protected by the best bullpen arms while four-plus leads are mopped up by weaker arms, so favorites win by exactly one or two more often than a normal model suggests.
mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.measurement: For each team over the last 2 seasons: runs allowed per inning in innings 7-9 by lead bucket (tie/within1, 2-3, 4+) and by reliever tier (top-3 by leverage index vs rest). Shrink bucket runs allowed to league with k = 100 innings. Combine with the margin distribution through a Markov simulation in innings 7-9: P(margin change | state). Units: run-allowed rate by state. As-of: bullpen availability at lineup post.
free_sources: MLB Stats API play-by-play (leverage index, pitching changes)
raw_data: inning-level: team, inning, score diff, pitcher used, leverage index, runs allowed
mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.why: Distribution tail for run-line and margin contracts, as sketched in the existing run_dist hypothesis but without a measured input.

mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.label: Regular-season stakes and rest policy (clinched/eliminated status, rest-day probabilities, September roster behaviour)
mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.mechanism: Teams that have clinched or been eliminated rest regulars, shorten starters' leashes or run tryout lineups, which lowers team strength on that day relative to the full-strength baseline.
mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.rationale: Late-season games for clinched or eliminated teams are played by different hitters and a differently managed bullpen than the season-long ratings assume; lineup_strength_delta only sees this after the card posts, while starter handling and bullpen usage in meaningless games never flow through it. Postseason games have no such effect, so the input must be gated by game type.
mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.measurement: For each team-game compute (a) playoff-clinch and elimination flags from standings (magic number <= games remaining, or tragic number), (b) games_since_last_rest_day for each of the 9 regular-lineup hitters and their historical P(sit) when the team is clinched/eliminated/in a day-game-after-night-game, estimated over the prior 5 seasons with shrinkage k = 40 team-games, (c) starter innings expectation reduced by the team's historical clinched/eliminated leash shift. Output: expected regular-lineup PA share and expected starter innings; units are PA share and innings. As-of: the morning of the game, updated at lineup post. Set to neutral for postseason games.
free_sources: MLB Stats API standings and schedule
raw_data: daily standings with games back and magic/tragic numbers
team-game lineup cards with slot and hitter
rest-day history per hitter
mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.why: Fills the regular-season motivation gap for KXMLBGAME-type contracts (late-season starts, rested regulars) that rest_travel and series_context do not address.

interactions.mechanism: The effective pitching edge is the starter quality gap times the share of innings he covers plus the bullpen gap times the rest, so starter workload acts as a weight that changes with the specific starter and with postseason leashes. A better starter who goes five innings counts for less than the same gap over seven.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute innings-weighted pitching rating versus separate terms; compare win-probability log loss on postseason versus regular season.

interactions.mechanism: Confirmed-lineup changes matter conditional on the starter's hand and the slot of the missing hitter: a left-handed bat resting against a lefty starter is no loss, while a missing right-handed regular against a lefty is. The same absence has different run value by matchup.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact missing-hitter value with starter hand and slot; test whether the delta is better modelled with hand-specific projections.

interactions.mechanism: Home advantage concentrates in the late innings: home teams skip the bottom 9th when ahead and win tied games by last bat, so HFA enters margin strikes as truncation and win probability as a tie-resolution bonus, not as a uniform shift in run difference.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate HFA separately for innings 1-8 and 9+ from historical run margins; check effect on spread rungs.

interactions.mechanism: Large margins are compressed because trailing teams' pitchers are replaced with weaker arms only after the game is out of reach, while narrow leads are protected; the probability of covering a 1.5-run spread is therefore not monotone with a constant-variance model, and fatigued bullpens loosen the compression.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare spread-rung calibration for favorites by bullpen freshness and lead bucket.

interactions.mechanism: In a series the rotation order, rest days and short postseason leash switch the pitching mix between games, so game 1 and game 5 have different effective starter weights and series win probability is not a power of a single-game probability.
interactions.how_to_test: Backtest series winner probabilities from sequential game models versus constant single-game probability.

nonlinearities.shape: Logistic-like win probability in expected run difference (about 10% per run near evenly matched), with Pythagorean exponent near 1.8 concave in run ratio
nonlinearities.why: Win probability is a concave-then-saturating function of expected run difference, so large favorites gain progressively less per added run of edge.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating weight: the incremental weight on the starter flattens beyond about 6 innings
nonlinearities.why: The starter's share of innings is bounded and hooks are sharp, so adding workload past six innings adds little to team run prevention.

nonlinearities.shape: Regression coefficient falls with games played; partial pooling toward run-differential talent
nonlinearities.why: The reliability of record versus run-differential grows slowly, so shrinkage weights should depend on sample size nonlinearly.

nonlinearities.shape: Multiplicative scaling of run rate with dispersion scaling (variance rises with park factor)
nonlinearities.why: Hitter-friendly parks raise both the mean and variance of runs, which matters for margin tails.

contract.settlement_definition: Four series: single-game total (KXMLBTOTAL) pays Yes if the two teams collectively score more than the strike (for example 8.5 runs) in the listed game; team total (KXMLBTEAMTOTAL) pays Yes if the named team scores N or more runs (title 'over 7.5', rule '8+'); series total games (KXMLBSERIESGAMES) pays Yes if more than the strike of games (6.5) are played in the championship series; a separate series-game-total series is title-only. The sampled rules do not state whether extra-inning runs count, whether the bottom of the ninth that is not played changes anything, or how postponed, suspended and rain-shortened games settle.

mechanism.summary: Total runs are the sum of two teams' runs, each the sum over innings of a clustered run process. For a team, expected runs equal the opposing starter's run prevention over the innings he covers plus the bullpen's rate over the rest, applied to the lineup's strength against that starter's hand and arsenal, then scaled multiplicatively by park, wind, air density and the umpire's zone, with defense adjusting balls in play. The distribution is overdispersed because runs cluster in big innings that start from baserunners and are amplified by home runs and relievers entering. Totals are therefore not a symmetric band around a mean: thresholds near the median price the shape of the right tail, which depends on environment (Coors, wind blowing out) that changes variance as well as the mean. Structural details matter: the home team's bottom of the ninth is not played when it leads, extra innings add runs (with an automatic runner) if the contract counts them, and a postponed or shortened game changes the sum. Series total games is a different object, the length of a best-of-seven determined by game-level win probabilities and their dependence.

stages.name: Pitching matchup and workload
stages.description: Runs allowed by each pitching staff come first from the listed starter and how long he pitches, then from the relievers who finish. The starter's true-talent run prevention, innings expectation and the manager's leash determine the split, and a scratch of the listed starter changes the total by a large amount. Bullpen availability changes late-inning rates.
stages.distribution: Mixture over starter exit time (4-7 innings) and over bullpen composition; scratch risk as rare regime.

stages.name: Lineup offence and matchup
stages.description: Each team's offence is the confirmed nine facing the specific starter: handedness-specific wRC+, order slot weights, and contact quality versus the starter's profile. Defense and catcher framing shape balls in play and strikeouts on the pitching side.
stages.distribution: Per-team expected runs about 3.5-5.5 with sd of expectation uncertainty about 0.4 runs from lineup and starter information.

stages.name: Run-environment multipliers
stages.description: Park factors, altitude, wind direction relative to the park axis, temperature and humidity (air density), roof state, ball regime and the umpire's called zone scale run scoring multiplicatively; the day-specific deviation from park norms is the information, because the park average is already priced. Variance increases with run environment.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative on mean runs (about 0.85-1.35); heteroskedastic: variance grows with the environment.

stages.name: Run distribution, truncation and extras
stages.description: Realised totals are drawn from an overdispersed, inning-clustered distribution. The home team may not bat in the ninth; a tie after nine brings extra innings with an automatic runner that adds runs only if the contract counts them. The right tail of the total thresholds (10+ runs) is driven by big innings and weak-bullpen blowups.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed discrete (negative-binomial-like) per team, correlated positively across teams via shared park and weather; truncated by bottom-9 skip and extended by extras.

stages.name: Series length (series total games)
stages.description: The series total contract is not about runs but about how many games a best-of-seven lasts. It follows from per-game win probabilities with home-field pattern and starters, with dependence through unobserved team strength; the 6.5 strike makes it the probability that the series goes the full seven.
stages.distribution: Discrete (4-7) with probability of 7 about 20-30% for evenly matched teams; dependence across games widens the tails.

distribution_variance.note: Overdispersion of the inning-clustered run count plus truncation of the home half-innings by the walk-off rule.

coaching_scheme.note: Manager strategy (bunting, intentional walks, pitching changes) has effects on run scoring that are second-order relative to pitchers, lineups and park; no sampled contract wording interacts with a managerial rule in a way that changes the count of runs, and the leash effect is included under workload.

mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.label: Probability the home team's bottom of the ninth is skipped (home lead after 8.5) and its run-total effect
mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.mechanism: A home team ahead after the top of the ninth does not bat, so its runs and the game total are truncated relative to nine full innings.
mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.rationale: A total of 8.5 is often priced as if both teams bat nine innings; in games where the home team is ahead the home runs stop early, shifting probability toward under, and the truncation is correlated with favorite status and low total.
mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.measurement: P(skip) = P(home leads after 8.5 innings) from the run distribution: P(home leads after top of 9) computed by convolving inning-level scores through 8 innings plus the visitors' top-9 distribution. Expected truncation loss in total = P(skip) x E[home runs in a bottom-9 inning] (about 0.5 runs). Adjust the mean total by that amount and widen the lower tail. As-of: lineup post with projected win probability. Units: runs of expected truncation. WALK-OFF TRUNCATION: when the home team trails or is tied entering the bottom of the 9th (or an extra inning), the half-inning ends once it takes the lead, so remaining runs are lost; compute the home team's expected runs in that half under the stopping rule (capped at runs needed plus the homer exception) and apply the loss separately to the home team total (KXMLBTEAMTOTAL for the home side), which is truncated, versus the visitor total, which is not, and to the combined game total.
raw_data: linescore: runs by inning by team, innings played, home flag
mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.why: Directly changes total thresholds near the median, especially for strong home favorites, and is absent from the existing catalog.

mlb.extras_run_contribution.label: Expected runs added by extra innings, by rule regime (regular-season automatic runner vs postseason bases-empty) and contract scope
mlb.extras_run_contribution.mechanism: A game tied after nine adds extra half-innings; in the regular season each starts with a runner on second, in the postseason (to my knowledge, unverified for 2026) each starts with bases empty, so the runs added differ by regime; runs there count only if the contract counts them.
mlb.extras_run_contribution.rationale: About one game in ten adds a few runs, which matters for rungs near the median; if the contract excludes extras, then these runs must be removed and shortened-game and walk-off logic differ.
mlb.extras_run_contribution.measurement: E[extras runs] = P(level after nine complete innings) x E[total runs in extras | level]. Estimate runs per extra half-inning by regime: regular season with automatic runner (2020-2025 extras, about 0.9-1.1 runs per half-inning, shrunk to team offence with k = 50 half-innings); postseason or any bases-empty extras at about the league per-inning rate for tied late-inning bullpens (about 0.45-0.55 runs per half-inning, estimated from postseason and pre-2020 extra innings). The home half ends at the go-ahead run (walk-off stopping rule), so the home half contributes fewer runs than the visitor half. Use the regime flag from the game type (regular season vs postseason) and set to 0 if rules say regulation only. Units: expected runs. As-of: lineup post and contract text version.
free_sources: Retrosheet / MLB Stats API extra-inning data
raw_data: linescore with extra innings; runner-on-second indicator
mlb.extras_run_contribution.why: The existing catalog assumes extras count but the sampled rules are silent; the input keeps the dependence explicit and testable. Re-specified by regime because all sampled totals are postseason games, where the automatic runner is not used to my knowledge.

mlb.series_length_distribution.label: Series length distribution (probability of 4/5/6/7 games) from game-level win probabilities with team-strength dependence
mlb.series_length_distribution.mechanism: A series total contract settles on how many games are played, a function of game win probabilities, home-field pattern and the dependence of games on a shared team-strength latent.
mlb.series_length_distribution.rationale: Using independent Bernoulli games understates the probability of sweeps and long series; team strength uncertainty and starter rotation make the sequence dependent, and short series compress the talent gap.
mlb.series_length_distribution.measurement: Simulate best-of-seven: game i win prob p_i from the single-game model with announced starters and rest (default 2-3-2 home pattern), draw team-strength offset ~ N(0, sd = 0.04 in win prob) shared across games, compute P(N=4,5,6,7). interactions.mechanism: Park factor, wind and air density multiply the same fly-ball carry, so in a hitter's park with a tailwind and thin air the effects compound; deviations from park norms, not absolute weather, carry the information, and the effect is largest for fly-ball-heavy lineups and starters.

interactions.mechanism: The total is a mixture of starter-run and bullpen-run innings, so the sensitivity of the total to starter quality depends on how long he goes, which depends on bullpen state and leash. A depleted bullpen lengthens the leash and thereby increases weight on the starter's quality.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact starter quality with exit-time distribution and bullpen freshness; check total residual by those terms.

interactions.mechanism: A smaller called zone raises walks and run scoring most for patient lineups against command-poor pitchers, and a larger zone helps pitchers with edge-heavy approach; umpire effect scales with the matchup's walk exposure rather than adding a fixed number of runs.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact umpire zone residual with lineup chase rate and pitcher zone rate in a walk model; test total residuals.

interactions.mechanism: In high-run environments variance rises faster than the mean (clustering of crooked-number innings), so the probability of totals above the market median falls less than a constant-variance model implies, and the under side is more exposed at low thresholds.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate dispersion as a function of park factor and wind-out indicator; compare calibration of thresholds near 10 runs in Coors versus pitcher's parks.

interactions.mechanism: Game-length regime: when the home team leads, the bottom of the ninth is skipped (negative total adjustment); when tied, extras add runs; when the home team trails, the game runs to completion. The three regimes sit at different parts of the run-difference distribution, so the expected total is a mixture with different slopes.
interactions.how_to_test: Condition historical totals on score state after eight innings and compare to unconditional total model.

nonlinearities.shape: Overdispersed negative-binomial tail: P(total >= 11) is several times a Poisson prediction
nonlinearities.why: Runs cluster in innings and crooked numbers amplify, so the right tail is heavy relative to a Poisson with the same mean; thresholds are priced in the tail.

nonlinearities.shape: Asymmetric saturating: out-blowing wind adds more carry than in-blowing wind removes, both saturate beyond about 15 mph
nonlinearities.why: Carry gains and losses at the wall are not symmetric and flatten at high wind speeds.

nonlinearities.shape: Roughly linear in density for HR carry, convex for hit-by-hit effects at altitude
nonlinearities.why: Reduced drag accumulates over a long flight, so the benefit rises more in the far outfield; Coors differs qualitatively.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex penalty for poor starters: a bad starter's extra runs per inning are larger because bullpen exposure grows and leverage rises
nonlinearities.why: A weak starter exits early, exposing the bullpen and raising run totals more than his rate gap alone suggests.

mechanism.summary: Runs in the first five innings are produced almost entirely by the two starters and their lineups, with the bullpen entering only after an early exit. Each starter faces the opposing order roughly twice, so the first five innings weight the top six hitters of each lineup more heavily than a nine-inning game does, and the times-through-the-order penalty applies across the second trip. The expected score per team is therefore the starter's run prevention over an exit-time distribution (an early pull exposes relievers) against the confirmed lineup by handedness, scaled by the park, weather and the umpire's zone, which is more influential early. Because the half-inning run process is clustered and discrete, five-inning margins are lumpy and ties are frequent enough that the winner, spread and total contracts differ materially: the winner market has a Tie strike, the spread a margin, the total a sum. Bullpen strength matters less than in the full game; starter leash and opener usage matter more. The sibling rules do not refund a starter change, so late scratches are priced risk.

stages.name: Listed starters and change risk
stages.description: Because the contract is not conditioned on the pitcher, the starter announced earlier might be replaced by another starter or an opener at any time before first pitch, and the market sits on the pre-announcement distribution until the lineup confirms. The distribution over actual starters is the first stage; its variance is large in postseason and when the listed pitcher is on a minor injury.
stages.distribution: Discrete mixture over starter identity with rare but high-impact switches; resolved at lineup post and first pitch.

stages.name: Starter run prevention across two trips
stages.description: Over the first five innings the starter faces the order about twice, and some starters a third time. Run prevention per trip falls for most pitchers on the second look, with a larger penalty for pitchers with few pitch types, while pitchers who exit before the fifth hand innings to relievers with a different rate. The mix over exit times is the key distribution.
stages.distribution: Mixture over exit time (about 4-6.5 innings); trip-specific run rates with second-trip penalty.

stages.name: Lineup slots weighted by first-five exposure
stages.description: In five innings each team sends about 21-23 batters to the plate, so slots 1-4 bat twice and often slots 5-6 twice if the offence is productive, while slots 7-9 are weighted less. The confirmed order and its handedness against the starter determine the weight on each hitter's skill set, and platoon advantages of the top of the order dominate.
stages.distribution: Slot exposure weights from a Markov chain; top-6 weight roughly 2/3 of PAs.

stages.name: Environment and zone early in the game
stages.description: Park dimensions, altitude, wind, temperature and the roof scale run scoring from the first pitch, and the plate umpire's zone is a large early-game effect because the early innings are pitched by the starters; contact quality and defense (balls in play) shape hits allowed.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative factor on run rate with higher variance in hitter-friendly parks; umpire effect about a few percent of runs.

stages.name: Discrete score distribution and tie mass
stages.description: The five-inning score is a pair of discrete overdispersed counts; the tie probability (about one game in eight) is the sum over equal scores and is sensitive to the total: low-total games tie more. The three contracts read this distribution differently (Tie strike, margin strikes, total strikes), so the model must output the full joint PMF.
stages.distribution: Skellam-like with extra clustering; tie mass concentrated at 0-0, 1-1, 2-2.

mlb.f5_starter_change_risk.rationale: Pre-lineup prices sit on the announced pitcher; a late scratch or opener plan is a large run-expectation change (a quality starter replaced by a bullpen day), and in the postseason pitching plans change.

mlb.f5_lineup_slot_exposure.label: Expected plate appearances by slot in innings 1-5 and slot-weighted matchup runs
mlb.f5_lineup_slot_exposure.mechanism: Within five innings the top of each order bats twice and the bottom less, so slots receive unequal weight.
mlb.f5_lineup_slot_exposure.rationale: Full-game wRC+ weights nine slots roughly evenly; F5 weight shifts toward the top six, and the weight on the top varies with team OBP (more baserunners, more PAs).
mlb.f5_lineup_slot_exposure.measurement: Markov-chain expected PA by slot in 5 innings given lineup OBP and starter allowed OBP: roughly (2.75, 2.65, 2.6, 2.5, 2.4, 2.3, 2.2, 2.1, 2.0) for a typical team, which sums to the team total of about 21.5 PA in five innings (about 4.3 PA per inning); slot weights are normalised to sum to the modelled team PA total. Slot-weighted runs per PA = sum slot weight x hitter run value vs starter hand (projection wOBA, k = 300 PA shrinkage). Units: expected runs in 5 innings against a typical starter. As-of: lineup post.

mlb.f5_reliever_innings_share.label: Expected share of the first five innings thrown by relievers (early exit) and their quality
mlb.f5_reliever_innings_share.mechanism: Early starter exits push relievers into innings 4 and 5; the mixture shifts F5 runs.
mlb.f5_reliever_innings_share.rationale: Starter-only models understate runs when the starter has a short leash, and bullpen quality (not starter) then governs the end of the F5 window; openers make the share large.
mlb.f5_reliever_innings_share.measurement: From the starter hazard of exit (see leash) compute E[outs by reliever in innings 1-5] = 15 - E[min(starter outs, 15)]; relief quality from the likely first reliever and leverage; F5 reliever share = that/15. F5 runs = starter rate x share_starter + reliever rate x share_relief. Uses 5 seasons start logs, k = 8 starts shrinkage to team average. Units: outs and runs per out. As-of: lineup post.

mechanism.summary: An inning is a short Markov process over base-out states: batters come up in lineup order, each plate appearance moves the state, and the half-inning ends after three outs, giving a zero-inflated run distribution whose probability of at least one run is about a quarter to a third. For the first inning the three or four hitters due up at the top of each order face the starter's first trip, so the probability of a run in the first inning (RFI) is the union of two half-innings driven by top-of-order on-base and power skill, handedness, and the starter's first-inning command. Later-inning markets depend on which batters are due, the times-through-the-order effect and which reliever enters; the ninth inning is special because the home team may not bat and the pitcher is usually a high-leverage reliever chosen by game state. Cumulative-inning markets (first 3, 5, 7) sum innings with a discrete tie mass. A first-principles model is a plate-appearance simulation with base-out states and pitcher-specific, count-based outcome probabilities, with strong shrinkage because inning-split samples are tiny. The ledger also files extras and a season longest winning streak here, each of which has a distinct mechanism.

stages.name: Which hitters and which pitcher are in the inning
stages.description: The first inning is deterministic in who bats first: slots 1-3 of the visiting side against the starter, then 1-3 of the home side, with slot 4 and 5 appearing only if baserunners accumulate. Ninth-inning markets instead depend on the due-up slots at that point and on the pitcher chosen by score state (closer, setup, mop-up), neither known pregame. The identity and handedness of these few players is the dominant information.
stages.distribution: Deterministic for first inning, mixture over due-up slots and reliever identity for later innings.

stages.name: Half-inning base-out Markov process
stages.description: From the bases-empty, zero-out state each PA transitions among states according to the batter-pitcher outcome probabilities (walk, single, double, home run, strikeout, ball in play out); the half-inning ends at three outs. P(at least one run) is the probability of leaving the zero-run absorbing path, and expected runs per inning follow. The top three hitters' OBP and extra-base power set the entry probability and the pitcher's early command sets walks.
stages.distribution: Zero-inflated geometric-like run count per half-inning (P(0) around 0.7 to 0.75), heavier tail when runners accumulate.

stages.name: First-trip pitcher state and zone
stages.description: The starter's first trip through the order combines fresh stuff with command variance; early innings also have an umpire-zone effect and park/weather shifts, but historical first-inning splits for a single pitcher are noisy (about 30 starts per season), so inference needs heavy shrinkage toward the pitcher's PA-level skill rather than first-inning ERA.
stages.distribution: Small-sample noise dominates observed first-inning splits; true variation across pitchers is small relative to sampling error.

stages.name: Game-state conditioning for late innings
stages.description: The ninth inning depends on score entering it: tied, one-run, save situation, blowout; the home team skips the bottom of the ninth when leading; pitcher choice follows leverage. The cumulative first 3/5/7 markets add innings and a tie mass whose probability depends on the score distribution at that point, with starters pulled and bullpens used in between. The F3/F5/F7 contracts filed here need starter-exit hazard, starter-change risk and slot-weighted five-inning exposure; those inputs (f5_starter_change_risk, f5_lineup_slot_exposure, f5_reliever_innings_share) are defined in first5_markets and are NOT claimed here. The bottom of the ninth is a stopping-rule process: the half-inning ends the moment the home team takes the lead, so home runs in that half are truncated (for a non-homer walk-off only the runs needed to lead count), which biases a naive over-1.5 or Tie estimate.
stages.distribution: State-dependent mixture; tie mass of cumulative scores about 15-25% for F3 and F5 depending on total.

stages.name: Extras variant (cross-referenced)
stages.description: The extras contract (KXMLBEXTRAS) is a regulation-tie event driven by the inning-by-inning run chain and is specified in extras_and_delay, where it belongs. The season-long longest-winning-streak contract (KXMLBWSTREAK) is an extreme-value object over 162 games and 30 teams that does not share inning mechanics; its input is defined in the unreg counting-specials record. This stage only carries the run distribution so extras tie mass is consistent with the cumulative-inning markets.
stages.distribution: Extras is a Bernoulli event with base rate near 8-10 percent of games; no inning-level streak distribution is modelled here.

pace_volume.note: Batters per inning and inning-index scoring.

distribution_variance.note: Inning zero-inflation and cumulative tie mass; the season-streak extreme value is no longer claimed here.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: The inning contracts sampled here (9th inning, first inning, first 3/5/7) are single-game events whose schedule and motivation effects act only through the lineup and bullpen already listed; the season-long streak that carried this category was moved out.

settlement_contract.note: Per-series wording: 9th-inning void, Tie strike, extras, streak split.

mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.label: First-inning run probability from a base-out Markov chain with the confirmed top-4 hitters and the starter's first-trip PA outcome rates
mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.mechanism: RFI is the union of two half-innings; each is a Markov process over the first four or five hitters.
mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.rationale: First-inning ERA or RFI history is nearly pure noise; a chain built from PA-level outcome probabilities (not inning-level results) uses all the data and the confirmed order, and includes the fact that the fourth and fifth hitters bat only if the first three reach.
mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.measurement: For each half-inning: transition probabilities for batter slots 1-5 from log5-combined P(walk), P(1B), P(2B+), P(HR), P(K), P(other out) using hitter vs hand rates (shrunk to projection k = 250 PA) and starter first-time-through rates (starter first-trip PA outcomes over last 2 seasons, shrunk to league k = 300 BF). Solve the chain analytically: P(no run) = path probabilities to three outs without scoring. RFI = 1 - P(no run top) x P(no run bottom); P(top run) and P(bottom run) also output for team-specific markets. Units: probability. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: PA-level outcomes by batter and pitcher; pitcher first-trip subset; lineup slots
mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.why: Replaces first_inning_splits as a computational estimand and removes dependence on 30-start samples.

mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.label: Ninth-inning entry state (score margin, home-bats flag) and expected pitcher and due-up slots
mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.mechanism: The 9th inning's run distribution depends on whether the home team bats, the margin, and who pitches.
mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.rationale: KXMLBINNINGTOTAL and KXMLBINNINGWIN settle on the ninth only, including the case where the home team skips the bottom. The probability that the bottom of the ninth is played falls with home-team lead probability, and the pitcher is the closer in save situations or a mop-up arm in blowouts.
mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.measurement: P(home bats bottom 9) = P(home not leading after top 9) from the run distribution after 8 innings and top-9 runs. Margin entering 9 from simulated score distribution (innings 1-8). Pitcher: P(closer) = P(save situation: lead 1-3 for the home team entering visitor's top? (visitors pitching vs home)); for the visitor's top 9 the pitcher is the home team's closer if home leads by <=3, otherwise a setup/mop-up arm. Closer availability from usage in prior 2 days (back-to-back/3-in-4 flags). Due-up slots from expected PAs through eight innings (0-8 batters). Output: expected runs in top-9 and bottom-9 and P(any run). As-of: lineup post (prior) and live updates. WALK-OFF STOPPING RULE: bottom-9 (and later) runs are computed from a half-inning chain that terminates when the home team takes the lead. Tied entering the bottom: P(any run) = P(chain reaches a go-ahead run), and the run count is 1 unless the final hit is a home run (then 1 + runners on). Home trailing by d: only the first d+1 runs can score, again with the homer exception. This truncated distribution, not the untruncated half-inning run distribution, feeds KXMLBINNINGTOTAL over 1.5 and the Tie strike of KXMLBINNINGWIN.
free_sources: MLB Stats API play-by-play (leverage, pitching changes)
raw_data: inning-level: score diff entering 9, pitcher used, inning runs, closer usage history
mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.why: The ninth is a state-conditional, non-exchangeable inning; no existing catalog input captures the skipped-bottom and closer selection.

mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.label: Team scoring and allowed-runs profile by inning index (1st versus 2nd-8th)
mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.mechanism: Offence is stronger early (top of order due up) and weaker late (relievers, platoon-optimised matchups).
mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.rationale: League scoring in the first inning exceeds other innings because the best hitters bat; team and park differences in first-inning versus other-inning scoring are mostly noise but have systematic pieces (starter quality, lineup top-heaviness).
mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.measurement: Per team: runs per half-inning for innings 1, 2-3, 4-6, 7-9 over last 3 seasons, shrink to league-by-inning k = 100 half-innings. Use for baseline; for team-pair adjust multiplicatively by opponent (ratio to league). Units: runs per half-inning. As-of: prior game.
raw_data: inning-level runs by team, park, home/away
mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.why: Provides the base rate by inning index and a ceiling for how much inning-specific tendency is real.

mlb.first_inning.reason: Baseline RFI rate by park/league is a prior; observed first-inning scoring history is noisy and should not drive the model alone. Overlaps mlb.first_inning_splits (WEAK, f3_split DUPLICATE); only the park/league RFI base rate is kept, as a prior.

mlb.first_inning_splits.reason: Starter first-inning ERA splits are sample-starved (about 30 innings a year); useful only after heavy shrinkage toward PA-level skill, as the catalog itself concedes.

mlb.lineup_pit.reason: The first three or four hitters of each side decide RFI; confirmed order is the central information.

mlb.platoon.reason: Handedness of the top four against the starter matters but is part of PA-level matchup probabilities.

mlb.sp_quality.reason: Starter true talent for the first trip; separate from first-inning splits.

mlb.plate_discipline.reason: Walk and zone rates feed baserunner probability; overlaps with k_rates but distinct outcome.

mlb.k_rates.reason: Strikeouts remove baserunner chances; partially duplicated by SP quality.

mlb.f3_split.reason: First-three-innings split is a larger-sample version of the same starter-top-of-order concept, with identical noise caveats.

mlb.tto.reason: Relevant for later innings (2nd-trip) and F5/F7 markets, not the first inning.

mlb.bullpen.reason: Reliever availability determines the 9th-inning and late-inning pitcher; drives inning-level markets late.

mlb.park.reason: Run environment scales first-inning probability by a few percent.

mlb.weather_pit.reason: Weather has small effects at inning level and is mostly captured in park norms.

mlb.umpire.reason: Zone effects early; modest for one inning.

mlb.run_dist.reason: Needed for cumulative tie mass and ninth-inning entry state; per-inning distribution required.

m.rules_text.reason: Series differ widely (void rules, Tie strike, skipped ninth), so wording per series decides the object.

mlb.babip_luck.reason: BABIP regression at inning scale is meaningless; relevant only to the rate estimates feeding the Markov chain. Removed from stage s2 inputs by resolver; no inning-scale use remains.

interactions.mechanism: A run in the first inning requires baserunners from the top three and then enough extra-base power or walks to convert, so the probability depends on the product of leadoff on-base skill, the number-three hitter's power and the pitcher's walk rate rather than their sum. A lineup top with two high-OBP hitters against a command-poor starter compounds.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare RFI log loss from the chain (product) versus additive top-three wOBA models.

interactions.mechanism: The ninth-inning run distribution has three regimes: save situation with closer (low run probability), tied or one-run with high-leverage arms, and blowout with mop-up arms; home-bats flag changes whether the bottom exists. The regime probabilities come from the score distribution, so ninth-inning markets are a mixture priced by margin.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate P(run in top-9) by entry margin bucket and closer availability; compare with unconditional average.

interactions.mechanism: Whether the ninth is played at all, and how many runs it can contain, depends on the margin entering the bottom half: a home lead removes it, a tie or one-run deficit ends it at the go-ahead run, and the due-up hitters set how often that run arrives. The truncation lowers over-1.5 and Tie-strike probabilities relative to the untruncated half-inning run distribution, most for tied games with a high-OBP due-up group.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare observed bottom-9 run distributions for tied-entering and trailing-entering games against the untruncated Markov chain output, split by due-up OBP tercile.

interactions.mechanism: Platoon advantage of the top of the order is conditional on the starter's pitch arsenal: a lefty-heavy top against a right-hander with a good changeup differs from the same top against a slider-only right-hander; the effect is realised in the first trip where hitters have not adjusted.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact top-four handedness share with starter changeup/slider usage in a first-trip PA model.

interactions.mechanism: Cumulative F3, F5 and F7 scores combine innings with different pitchers; tie probability depends on the joint distribution of both teams' runs across the change from starter to bullpen, which shifts with exit time and bullpen state.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate cumulative score by inning with starter-to-bullpen switch and compare tie frequency across F3, F5, F7 with the data.

nonlinearities.shape: Zero-inflated, convex: P(run) rises convexly with top-three OBP because the chain compounds across hitters
nonlinearities.why: Extra baserunners make each later batter more valuable (runner-on states), so the probability of at least one run grows faster than linearly in on-base skill.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating weight with innings pitched: weight on pitcher-specific first-inning history rises slowly and stays low
nonlinearities.why: First-inning outcomes are rare events with heavy sampling noise; the shrinkage weight should grow roughly with the number of innings but remain small.

nonlinearities.shape: Discrete mass at 0 runs per inning (about 72%) with geometric tail
nonlinearities.why: Inning scores are zero-inflated so a normal approximation fails for 0.5 and 1.5 strikes.

nonlinearities.shape: Step by margin entering the ninth: save situation (lead 1-3) versus blowout
nonlinearities.why: Pitcher quality and run probability change discontinuously around the save-situation boundary.

nonlinearities.shape: Absorbing truncation: the bottom-9 run count is capped at the margin needed to take the lead (plus homer exception)
nonlinearities.why: The home half ends on the go-ahead run, so P(2+ runs in the bottom 9) is far below the untruncated chain value in tied or one-run games; this is a stopping-rule nonlinearity distinct from the save-situation step.
