contract.settlement_definition: No live series is classified under this archetype. The extras contract trades as KXMLBEXTRAS (filed under the inning archetype): Yes if at least one extra inning is played in the named game, i.e. the game is tied after regulation; the delay contract trades as KXMLBDELAY (filed under off-field): Yes if the game originally scheduled for the date is officially delayed due to weather, including a delayed start and any suspension or stoppage after the start, while non-weather delays (for example power or crowd) do not count. Treatment of suspended games and of games postponed (rather than delayed) is not stated in the sampled text. Sibling-filed rules text (verbatim, not usable as rules_evidence because the ledger files the tickers elsewhere): KXMLBEXTRAS 'If at least 1 extra inning is played in the Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay professional baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 28, 2026, then the market resolves to Yes.'; KXMLBDELAY 'officially delayed due to weather. This includes a delayed start time as well as any suspension or stoppage of play after the event has begun due to weather.' Claims about both contracts are conditional on the ledger re-keying; this archetype has no live series of its own.
variants_and_edge_cases: The two contract families are unrelated mechanically: extras is a function of the run distribution (a regulation tie), delay is a weather-timing event unrelated to team quality, and a shared model would conflate them.

Delay definition counts both a delayed start time and any in-game weather stoppage regardless of duration, so even short (five-minute) stoppages count if recorded as official delays; a postponed game (no first pitch that day) is not described.

Extras requires the game to remain tied after the top and bottom of the ninth (the bottom is played only if the home team does not lead); a game called by weather while tied before the ninth is a suspension or shortened game, not extras.
A suspended game completed later with extra innings is attached to 'originally scheduled' date in the sibling wording but handling is unstated.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official linescore (innings played) for extras; official game log/box score delay record for weather delays (MLB Stats API, box score 'delay' line); not named in the sibling rules.

series_mapping_issues.issue: Extras contract is filed under first_inning_and_inning_markets in the ledger; rules text exists there ('If at least 1 extra inning is played in the Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay professional baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 28, 2026, then the market resolves to Yes.').

Weather-delay contract is filed under offfield_markets in the ledger; rules text exists there ('This market resolves to Yes if the Tampa Bay vs New York Pro Baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 7, 2026 is officially delayed due to weather.').

mechanism.summary: Two event families share the archetype and are mechanically unrelated. Extra innings occur when the two teams' nine-inning run totals are equal, so the probability is the tie mass of the difference of two overdispersed run counts, adjusted by the structure that the home team skips the bottom ninth when ahead; it is highest in low-scoring, evenly matched games and is a few percentage points higher than naive Poisson-based estimates because runs correlate positively across teams through park and weather. Delay markets are weather-timing problems: a delay requires precipitation, lightning within the league's safety radius, or severe wind/temperature conditions overlapping the game window while the roof is open or absent, and the umpire crew and team officials decide to stop or hold play. The probability depends on forecast timing and convective structure rather than team quality, and on how the contract defines delay (start versus in-game, any duration). Both are low-to-moderate probability events where the contract's exact wording and the quality of timing information decide edge.

stages.name: Regulation score distribution and tie mass
stages.description: Extras occur only if the score is level after nine complete innings. The tie mass is the sum over k of P(away = k) P(home = k) with a positive dependence between teams, so a low expected total and a close pairing raise it. The home team's skipped bottom of the ninth does not create extras; it removes them in games where the home team leads.
stages.distribution: Tie probability about 8-10% of games; sensitive to total: low-total games tie more; positive team-run correlation raises tie mass.

stages.name: Late-inning resolution before extras
stages.description: Extras happen when the score is level after nine complete innings. The main routes are a tie after the top of the 9th that the home team fails to break, and a one-or-more-run visitor lead that the home team equalises without taking the lead; a home lead after 8.5 innings removes the bottom half entirely. The bottom-9 half-inning is a stopping-rule process: it ends the moment the home team takes the lead, so run totals are truncated and the P(level) depends on the closer, the due-up hitters and the deficit entering the half.
stages.distribution: Conditional probability of the home team scoring at least once in a tied bottom 9 is roughly 27-32% for a typical reliever (league P(run) per half-inning is about 0.27); lower against elite closers. The extras event is Bernoulli with a mixture over the entering run differential.

stages.name: Weather exposure over the game window
stages.description: Delay requires weather in the window: precipitation timing relative to first pitch and the expected 3-hour game, lightning within eight miles (league and stadium safety rules), heavy wind or cold in some venues, and a roof that is open, closed, or retractable with a decision made before first pitch. The same forecast yields different delay probabilities across parks with and without roofs and with different drainage.
stages.distribution: Binary event with probability about 5-10% overall, near 0 in domes and up to 30-50% on convectively active evenings.

stages.name: Decision and recording process
stages.description: Whether weather becomes an official delay depends on umpire and home-team judgement and on the way the delay is recorded: a start delayed by tarp, an in-game stoppage, a rain-shortened or suspended game, or a postponement. Short delays may not be recorded in the structured data, and a postponed game is not a delayed one under the sibling wording.
stages.distribution: Threshold decision with human judgement; recording rules produce a minimum recorded duration in data.

stages.name: Interaction between the two events
stages.description: Extras lengthen the game and thereby increase exposure to in-game weather delays, so a delay contract that counts in-game stoppages is mildly positively related to extras; start-delay contracts are unaffected. For the extras contract, a suspended game (weather) tied in the middle is not extras.
stages.distribution: Small positive dependence through game length; negligible for start delays.

talent_strength.note: Run-prevention quality drives total and tie mass.

efficiency_conversion.note: Conversion of the home half-inning into a walk-off run.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Game length exposure for in-game delays.

role_personnel.note: Neither event depends on which individual players start beyond what the run distribution already captures; delays depend on weather and officials rather than roster composition, and extras on aggregate scoring, so no separate personnel driver is needed.

availability_news.note: Confirmed starters and scratches enter through sp_quality (as-of lineup post), the roof open/closed decision through roof_state, and postponement/forecast updates through forecast_precip_timing; lineup-card vintage is tracked as an open item (ext_lineup_vintage).

pace_volume.note: Pace of play affects when the bottom of the ninth is reached and game duration, but not the tie probability or delay occurrence in a way sampled contracts can price, so no pace driver is added.

mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.label: Tie probability after nine innings from joint (correlated) run distributions
mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.mechanism: The tie mass depends on the correlation of the two teams' runs through park and weather and on the discrete shapes.
mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.rationale: Independent-NB convolution underestimates ties because shared park/weather effects make both teams' totals move together; high-scoring environments widen the distribution and lower tie mass per run level.
mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.measurement: Compute P(tie after 9) = sum_k P(R_a=k, R_h=k) from a bivariate NB or copula with correlation rho_park calibrated on 10 seasons of games by park (shrink k = 300 games) and by wind-out indicator; adjust for home team skipping bottom 9 (P(home leads after 8.5) removes some games). Calibrate against observed extras rate by expected-total decile. Units: probability. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: game-level: runs by team, innings played, park, wind, temperature
mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.why: KXMLBEXTRAS settles on the tie event, so the joint distribution (not each team's total) is the right object.

mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.label: P(extra innings) from the inning-by-inning score chain, including tie-restoring bottom-9 halves
mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.mechanism: Extras occur whenever the score is level after nine complete innings (or after the home half is played to its end), so the event is a function of the joint inning-by-inning chain, not of a single tied-entering-the-ninth conditional.
mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.rationale: KXMLBEXTRAS pays when at least one extra inning is played. Games reach extras by two routes: tied after the top of the 9th with the home team failing to score, and visitors leading after the top of the 9th with the home team tying the score but not taking the lead (the half-inning ends on the third out, not on the tying run). Modelling only the first route understates P(extras); the home walk-off stopping rule also truncates the bottom-9 run distribution.
mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.measurement: P(extras) = sum over states s of P(state s entering bottom 9) x P(home half-inning ends with score level), computed from an inning-by-inning Markov chain: states are (run differential after top 9, outs=0) with visitor closer PA rates (shrunk to league reliever rates, k = 150 BF) and home due-up hitters. Tied entering bottom 9: P(level) = P(home scores 0). Home trailing by d>=1: P(level) = P(home scores exactly d runs without taking the lead, the half ends on the third out). Home leading: no bottom 9, P(extras)=0. Walk-off stopping rule applied, so the half-inning ends once the home team takes the lead. Validate on 5 seasons by comparing predicted and observed extras rate by pre-game expected-total decile. Units: probability. As-of: confirmed lineups.
raw_data: half-inning-level: tied entering bottom 9 flag, pitcher, due-up slots, runs scored
mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.why: Defines P(extras) as P(level score after nine complete innings) so both extras routes are included.

mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.label: Lightning-proximity exposure within the league's 8-mile safety radius over the game window
mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.mechanism: Lightning within a set radius triggers mandatory delays independent of rain amount.
mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.rationale: A forecast of rain probability misses thunderstorms with sparse precipitation; lightning radius rules cause delays even when the field is dry, and conversely rain can come without lightning and be played through.
mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.measurement: From a lightning-strike archive (GOES-R GLM or NLDN), compute historical frequency of strikes within 8 miles of the park during the 3.5-hour window by month and local-hour; combine with the forecast CAPE/convective probability from the forecast vintage via logistic regression calibrated on 5 seasons of recorded delays. Output P(lightning within 8 mi in game window). As-of: 3 hours before first pitch and update at lineup post. Units: probability. ASSUMPTION: the 8-mile radius and 30-minute hold are common convention (stadium or umpire discretion); MLB publishes no uniform league rule. GOES-R GLM gives optical flashes, not NLDN strikes, so archive-based frequencies are a proxy.

mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.why: Distinguishes lightning-driven from rain-driven delays and sharpens the weather gate.

mlb.official_delay_record_definition.rationale: If delays under about ten minutes are not recorded in the box score or play-by-play, history underestimates the event, and the question of whether a five-minute tarp pause counts is a contract question.
mlb.official_delay_record_definition.measurement: From 5 seasons of MLB Stats API gamefeed and box-score notes: distribution of recorded delay duration; share of games with delay > 10, 30, 60 minutes; compare with weather-station precipitation timing at the park to estimate unrecorded stoppages (rain during play with no delay). Output P(recorded | rain in window) by duration bucket. SOURCE_UNVERIFIED for completeness of recording. Units: probability.

mlb.official_delay_record_definition.why: Defines the empirical event frequency and tests the sensitivity of the market to the recording threshold.

interactions.mechanism: Extras probability is the diagonal of the joint score distribution; shared park and weather push both teams' runs the same way, increasing diagonal mass at any given total. The effect is largest in extreme parks where the common factor is largest.

interactions.mechanism: Delay probability is the product of weather overlapping the window and the roof being open; for retractable roofs the decision to close depends on forecast confidence, so closed-roof parks have near-zero delay, and the gating is a regime switch. Lightning adds delays on dry fields.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate P(delay) with roof-type interaction and lightning indicator; compare calibration by roof type.

interactions.mechanism: Extras equal tie after top 9 times failure to walk off; the failure probability depends on closer quality, so for elite closers the extras probability is lower for the same tie probability.
interactions.how_to_test: Decompose extras frequency into tie and non-walk-off components and test closer effect.

interactions.mechanism: If the delay contract counts in-game stoppages, game length (including extras) increases exposure; if it counts only start delays, extras are irrelevant. The wording switches the dependence regime between the two events.

interactions.mechanism: Recorded delays follow a threshold in precipitation intensity and duration; light drizzle is played through while heavy rain triggers a tarp, so the response of delay probability to rain probability is steeply nonlinear above a threshold.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit logistic of recorded delay on forecast precipitation intensity and duration; test breakpoint.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold/saturating: delay probability low below about 30% precipitation chance, steep between 40-70%, saturating near 90%
nonlinearities.why: Delay requires rain or lightning to actually occur during play and be heavy enough, so the response to forecast probability is S-shaped.

nonlinearities.shape: Tie mass peaks at low totals: P(tie) falls convexly as expected total rises
nonlinearities.why: The diagonal of the joint distribution thins as variance grows, so tie probability is decreasing and convex in expected total.

nonlinearities.shape: Binary gate: closed roof reduces delay probability to near zero regardless of forecast
nonlinearities.why: The roof removes exposure, so weather inputs matter only when open.

nonlinearities.shape: Approximate threshold (assumed convention): a strike within about 8 miles commonly triggers a roughly 30-minute hold, independent of strike count
nonlinearities.why: League safety protocol makes delay a step function of lightning proximity rather than intensity. This is an assumed convention, not a published uniform MLB rule; the threshold distance and hold length vary by stadium and umpire crew.

contract.settlement_definition: No MLB announcer-mention series appears in the series ledger and no rules text was sampled, so the settlement object cannot be stated from evidence: for a word-mention market the YES condition would be that a named word or phrase is spoken in a specified broadcast, but which feed (national, home, away, radio, Spanish-language), which speakers, whether pre/post-game segments count, whether on-screen graphics or sponsor reads count, how plural or inflected forms count, and what happens in a delay, postponement or extra innings are all unknown.
variants_and_edge_cases: Feed ambiguity: a national telecast, a regional sports network home feed and an away feed have different crews and vocabularies; the contract's named source decides which crew's language rate applies.
Counting rules (exact word versus stem, spoken versus on-screen, ad reads, replay clips, pre- and post-game shows) change the effective exposure by large factors and are unknown for MLB.
Broadcast length varies with game duration, extra innings and delays, so exposure time is itself random, and a postponed or suspended game restarts the clock.
Event-triggered words (player milestones, injuries, umpire controversies) have near-zero base rate that jumps if the trigger occurs; the market is a mixture over trigger realisation.
contract.settlement_data_source: Unknown: presumably a transcript or video review by Kalshi's resolver of the named broadcast; no MLB series or rule text sampled to confirm.

mechanism.summary: A word-mention market is a count of spoken occurrences in an exposure window, settled Yes if the count is at least one. The generating process is a point process: each crew has a baseline per-hour rate for each word, shaped by its vocabulary and by the broadcast format (national versus local, play-by-play versus color), multiplied by the length of the broadcast (nine innings take about two and a half to three hours, extras and delays extend it), plus event-triggered bursts when game events make the word relevant (a no-hitter in progress, a milestone, weather, injuries, the name of a player who comes to bat). Baseball statistics offer weak direct signal; most of the information is which crew is on the air, what the game script will produce, and who the players of interest are. Occurrences cluster because topics persist, so counts are overdispersed and the probability of at least one is lower than the Poisson at the same mean for low-rate words and higher for topic-driven words. Little structured data exists, so the quality of any prior depends on building transcripts.

stages.name: Which broadcast and crew
stages.description: The contract names a broadcast; its crew (play-by-play announcer, color analyst, sideline reporter), network (national such as Fox, ESPN, TBS, or the local regional network) and language determine the vocabulary and the style. National postseason crews differ from local crews in word choice, in discussion of rivalry and in sponsor language. The same game can have different feeds with very different base rates.
stages.distribution: Categorical crew identity with heterogeneous base-rate distributions; crew changes (injury or schedule) rare but discrete.

stages.name: Exposure time
stages.description: The window is the broadcast, which runs from first pitch to the final out plus any specified pre- and post-game segments; time depends on pace of play, pitching changes, extras and weather delays. Exposure is random: a seven-inning game or a delayed game changes the available time by tens of minutes, and a game called early shortens it.
stages.distribution: Right-skewed duration (about 2.4 to 3.2 hours typical; delays add up to hours); extras add about 15-20 minutes per inning.

stages.name: Word base rate per crew
stages.description: Given exposure, the count of a specific word follows a point process with a crew-specific rate per hour; common baseball words are near-certain to occur, while rare or topical words have rates below one per game. Rates differ by crew because of verbal habits (frequent use of 'Statcast', specific player nicknames, sponsor read phrases).
stages.distribution: Poisson-like with overdispersion; zero-inflated for rare words; per-crew rate heterogeneity.

stages.name: Triggered topics and named entities
stages.description: Words referring to events or people occur only when the game or the news makes them relevant: a pitcher's perfect game attempt, a milestone, a player returning from injury, a trade, weather, an umpire dispute, a rivalry. Names of players are used in proportion to their involvement (plate appearances, pitching) and storylines. These are bursts above the base rate with probabilities that depend on game events and pregame narratives.
stages.distribution: Event-triggered bursts: probability of word given trigger is high, trigger probability low; mixture structure.

stages.name: Counting rules and clustering
stages.description: What counts (inflections, spoken versus displayed, ads) changes the effective exposure and rate; counts cluster because once a topic is introduced it is repeated, so the distribution is overdispersed and the probability of at least one relative to the mean is shape-dependent. The settlement resolver's counting also introduces measurement noise.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed (negative-binomial or self-exciting) count; P(count >= 1) depends on dispersion parameter and zero mass.

mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.label: Crew-specific word and phrase rate per broadcast hour with dispersion (transcript-based)
mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.mechanism: Each crew has a characteristic per-hour rate for each lexeme and a dispersion beyond Poisson.
mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.rationale: The catalog's mention_text names crew language tendencies without a measurement; the question needs per-word per-crew rates and a dispersion estimate because probability of at least one is concave in the rate and depends on clustering.
mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.measurement: From transcripts (ASR with timestamps) of 40+ games per crew: for each word w count n_gw and exposure hours t_g; fit negative-binomial n_gw ~ NB(mean = t_g * lambda_cw, dispersion phi_cw) with lambda_cw shrunk to national lexeme rate with k = 6 games and phi pooled by word class. Stemming rules follow the contract text version. P(at least one) = 1 - integrated NB zero probability given expected exposure. As-of: before first pitch with crew known.
free_sources: Own ASR transcripts of broadcast audio
Closed captions from MLB.TV or broadcast (SOURCE_UNVERIFIED)
raw_data: game-crew-word counts with timestamps and exposure hours; crew assignments
mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.why: The market is a Poisson-like exposure market with crew-specific rates; without these the probability is unanchored.

mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.label: Broadcast airtime distribution (game duration with delay and extras scenarios, plus included pre/post segments)
mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.mechanism: Exposure is the time on air, a random variable depending on pace, extras, delays and scheduling.
mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.rationale: The mention count scales with airtime, but airtime is uncertain: from a pitch-clock game of 2h25m to a 4h delayed extra-inning game, and pre/post segments may be inside or outside the contract window.
mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.measurement: Simulate duration = base minutes (team pair mean time per game, 2023+ pitch-clock regime, half-life 60 games) + 17 minutes x extra innings + delay minutes with probability from delay_risk; shift for pre-game and post-game windows if counted. Output distribution of exposure hours. Shrink team-pair means to league with k = 25 games. As-of: lineup post. Units: hours.
raw_data: game-level: duration, innings, delays, start time, network schedule
mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.why: Converts a per-hour word rate into a per-game probability.

mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.label: Player and team name mention rate as a function of involvement (PA, pitching, storyline salience)
mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.mechanism: Names are said when players are in the action or in the news, in proportion to involvement.
mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.rationale: A market on a specific player's name depends on whether he plays, bats in high-leverage spots, pitches, is injured or traded; base-rate tables for common baseball words do not apply.
mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.measurement: Model: mentions of player p per game = a_p x (PA_p + BF_p) + b_p x storyline_flag(p) with a_p estimated from 30+ transcribed games shrunk to role-class (star, regular, bench, pitcher) k = 10 games; storyline_flag from news on the previous 3 days (injury return, milestone, award talk). Zero when the player is not active. Units: mentions per game. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: transcript mentions by player; lineup and PA; news flags
mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.why: Name-based markets are driven by involvement, not by baseball skill statistics.

mlb.sponsor_read_inventory.label: Scripted sponsor/promo read inventory and tagline language by network
mlb.sponsor_read_inventory.mechanism: Sponsor reads and promos are repeated at fixed cadence and contain fixed vocabulary.
mlb.sponsor_read_inventory.rationale: Words from sponsor segments have near-deterministic rates if the contract counts them; unknown whether they count, but they inflate the rates for brand names and phrases.
mlb.sponsor_read_inventory.measurement: From transcripts: segments classified as sponsor read via keyword templates (for example 'presented by', 'brought to you by'); per-network reads per half-hour and vocabulary, scheduled by network and time. Rate of word w in reads = reads per hour x P(w in read text). Units: occurrences per hour. As-of: network schedule for the date.

interactions.mechanism: Topical words occur at baseline until a trigger fires, after which the rate jumps; the market probability is the mixture P(trigger) x P(word|trigger) + (1-P(trigger)) x baseline. interactions.how_to_test: Condition word frequency on trigger flags in transcripts and test mixture versus homogeneous rate.

interactions.mechanism: National versus local feed and counting rules (sponsors, graphics) switch the effective vocabulary; a contract limited to the national feed uses a different crew and sponsor mix than the home feed, so probability is determined first by the regime then by the rate. interactions.mechanism: A player's name rate multiplies his involvement (PA, pitching) and the storyline salience (return from injury, award talk); a star in a storyline gets a rate several times a bench player's, and a non-starter gets zero, so involvement gates the storyline effect.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit mention-rate model with involvement x storyline interaction on transcripts.

interactions.mechanism: Delays and extras both lengthen the broadcast but are nearly independent events with different tails; the airtime distribution is a convolution with a heavy right tail, so rare-word probabilities have a fat contribution from long-game scenarios.

nonlinearities.shape: Overdispersion with zero inflation: P(0) far above Poisson for topical words
nonlinearities.why: Clustering and topic persistence make many games have none and a few have many, which changes P(at least one).

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold: probability jumps once the trigger occurs (no-hitter after the 6th inning, milestone in sight)
nonlinearities.why: Topical language is gated by event occurrence, producing a step in rate.

contract.settlement_definition: A grab-bag of contract families with different resolution events: award markets (KXMLBNLMOTY, KXMLBALMOTY manager of the year; KXMLBEOTY executive of the year) pay Yes if the named person wins the 2026 award; the team-sale market (KXMLBTEAMSALE) pays Yes if the named franchise is sold before a date and the deal is finalized and approved by the Governing League; the weather-delay market (KXMLBDELAY) pays Yes if the named game is officially delayed due to weather (start delay or later stoppage), with non-weather delays not counting; the esports match market (KXMLBBGAME, Mobile Legends) pays Yes on a named team winning a full match, with fair-price refunds if postponed beyond 48 hours, cancelled or forfeited before play. KXMLBCOACH (next manager) has only a title in the sample.

rules_evidence.quote: This market resolves to Yes if the Tampa Bay vs New York Pro Baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 7, 2026 is officially delayed due to weather.
rules_evidence.establishes: Weather-delay is a game-day weather event settled on an official delay record, mechanically the same as the delay half of the extras_and_delay archetype.

rules_evidence.quote: The deal must be finalized and approved by the Governing League to be encompassed by the Payout Criterion.
rules_evidence.establishes: Team-sale Yes requires league approval and closing before the deadline, not just an announced agreement, so approval-stage timing is the object.

rules_evidence.quote: If the relevant match is postponed and not started within 48 hours of its originally scheduled start time, the market will resolve to the fair market price.
rules_evidence.establishes: This KXMLB-prefixed market is an esports (Mobile Legends) match with a 48-hour postponement refund rule, unrelated to baseball.

rules_evidence.quote: If Don Mattingly wins the Pro Baseball National League Manager of the Year in the 2026 season, then the market resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: Manager-of-the-Year is a voted annual award settled on the official winner; one market per candidate.

variants_and_edge_cases: Family heterogeneity: awards (voter model), franchise sale (M&A approval hazard), weather delay (meteorology), next-manager (hiring hazard), esports match (rating model) have unrelated mechanisms and unrelated data; routing by series prefix is unsafe because KXMLBBGAME is Mobile Legends.

Awards: ties or co-winners are possible for some MLB awards but the sampled MOTY and EOTY rules do not state tie treatment (the WSMVP rule in another archetype pays $1/N), so tie handling for these is CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS.
Team sale: signed agreement, league committee review and approval vote, and closing are distinct milestones; the sampled rule demands finalization and league approval before the deadline.
Weather delay counts start delays and in-game stoppages but excludes non-weather delays; postponement without play is not described.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official league announcements (awards from BBWAA/league, franchise sale from league approval announcements), official game delay record, and esports league results (MPL); sources not otherwise named.

mechanism.summary: These markets share only the fact that they are not decided by the on-field result of a particular game. Each family has its own generating process. Awards are produced by a voter model: a ballot of writers ranks candidates on a mixture of performance (wins above expectation for managers, front-office construction for executives), narrative and team success, with finalists announced before winners and ballots cast before the postseason. Franchise sales follow an institutional pipeline (process, exclusivity, definitive agreement, committee review, owners' vote, closing), so the probability that a sale completes before a date is a hazard keyed to the current stage. Weather-delay markets are meteorology conditional on timing and roofs. The next-manager market is a hiring hazard conditional on a vacancy and the candidate pool. The esports match market is a rating-based match model unrelated to baseball. A single reference-class base rate for 'off-field' events is therefore close to meaningless, and each family needs its own information set and timing logic.

stages.name: Family routing and contract identification
stages.description: Before any modelling the contract family must be identified from the rules text rather than the prefix; the same ticker prefix includes awards, a franchise sale, a weather delay, an esports match and a hiring market. Routing determines which data and mechanism apply and prevents baseball inputs from being applied to the esports match.
stages.distribution: Categorical family label; misrouting yields entirely wrong features.

stages.name: Voter-model awards
stages.description: Manager and executive of the year are decided by a ballot of writers: managers of teams that exceed expectations (wins over preseason projection, division title, turnaround from a poor prior season) tend to win; executives are judged on roster construction; votes are cast before the postseason, so the final standings and the narrative at the end of the regular season are what matter. Finalists are information events and candidate sets are small.
stages.distribution: Few contenders with heavy concentration; win probability nonlinear in wins over expectation; ballot ties rare.

stages.name: Franchise-sale approval hazard
stages.description: A sale proceeds from a process (bids, exclusivity, definitive agreement) through league committee review and an owners' vote to closing. The probability of closing before a date depends on the current stage, the typical duration of each stage and the news cadence; rumor-stage deals complete much less often than signed deals awaiting league vote.
stages.distribution: Stage-dependent hazard with long, right-skewed durations; absorbing completion; many deals fail before signing.

stages.name: Weather-delay and calendar events
stages.description: The KXMLBDELAY market is a game-day weather event: it follows the forecast precipitation and lightning timing, the roof status and the team's and umpires' decisions, and has the same mechanism as the delay half of the extras and delay archetype. Calendar markets (opening day date) depend on league schedule announcements.
stages.distribution: Binary with probability driven by forecast timing; near-deterministic for scheduled calendar items.

stages.name: Esports match model and quotes as noise
stages.description: The Mobile Legends match is a team-rating problem: team strength (Elo/Glicko over recent matches), map or game-level win rates, roster and patch changes, and series format (best-of-3 versus best-of-5), none connected to baseball. Prices and external lines are only references.
stages.distribution: Binary with series-length compression of strength gap; rating uncertainty large for new rosters.

talent_strength.note: Award contender strength and esports team rating.

environment.note: Weather-delay market uses forecast data, to be routed to the extras_and_delay record; here only news is covered.

game_context_script.note: Not a game-outcome archetype; only stage-of-process news.

settlement_contract.note: Rules by family; refunds and approval conditions.

role_personnel.note: There is no single personnel structure across these families: voters, league approvers, esports rosters have different roles and are handled inside the family-specific inputs, so no common role/personnel category is defined.

coaching_scheme.note: Scheme and strategy do not enter any of these contracts except implicitly through managerial performance in awards, which is represented as wins over expectation; no tactical information changes the resolution of a sale, delay or esports match market in this archetype.

pace_volume.note: Opportunity counts (plate appearances, serve points) do not exist for these resolution events; the volume-like quantities are voting weights and match length, which are encoded in family-specific inputs.

efficiency_conversion.note: No per-opportunity conversion rate exists for sales, awards or delays; the nearest object is stage-conversion probability, treated as the hazard in the sale input.

officiating_rules.note: Official rule differences matter only through contract wording (approval, refunds, co-winners), which is covered under settlement; there are no officials whose tendencies alter these outcomes except the umpire's delay decision, handled in the delay record.

mlb.manager_wins_over_expectation.label: Manager/executive award score: wins over preseason expectation, division outcome and turnaround
mlb.manager_wins_over_expectation.mechanism: Awards for managers and executives are voted on surprise and success relative to expectation rather than on absolute record.
mlb.manager_wins_over_expectation.rationale: Votes correlate more with wins minus preseason projection (and a division title or big turnaround) than with wins alone; the voting ballot closes before the postseason, so late-season trajectory and awards-ballot deadline matter.
mlb.manager_wins_over_expectation.measurement: score = (actual wins - preseason projected wins, ZiPS/PECOTA/consensus) + 3 x division title flag + 2 x playoff berth + 0.5 x improvement vs prior season wins (scaled), computed at the ballot deadline; map to vote probability by multinomial logit calibrated on 15 seasons of finalist votes (shrink k = 3 seasons). Executive award adds payroll efficiency and offseason acquisitions. Units: composite score and probability. As-of: at ballot deadline and updated daily.
raw_data: season-level: team wins, projected wins (preseason), prior-year wins, division rank, award votes
mlb.manager_wins_over_expectation.why: Gives a concrete quantity for the voter model rather than a generic base rate.

mlb.sale_process_stage_hazard.label: Franchise-sale stage hazard: probability of closing and league approval before a date given process stage
mlb.sale_process_stage_hazard.mechanism: A franchise sale moves through stages with characteristic durations and failure probabilities.
mlb.sale_process_stage_hazard.rationale: Reports of 'agreement in principle' and 'definitive agreement signed' have very different completion odds and timelines; league review and owners' vote add months, and the sampled contract demands finalization and approval before the deadline.
mlb.sale_process_stage_hazard.measurement: Define stages: S0 rumored, S1 exclusive negotiation, S2 signed definitive agreement, S3 under league committee review, S4 owners' vote scheduled, S5 closed. Estimate stage-to-closing completion probability and duration distribution (log-normal or Weibull) from historical MLB sales (small N, about 15 over 20 years) and other major-league franchise sales, with Bayesian shrinkage to cross-league data. P(close before T) = sum over path of stage-duration convolution. As-of: latest credible report timestamp. Units: probability.
raw_data: deal-level: stage timestamps, announced approvals, closing date
mlb.sale_process_stage_hazard.why: KXMLBTEAMSALE settles only on finalization and approval, so stage and duration drive the probability.

mlb.mlbb_team_rating_series_format.label: Mobile Legends team rating (Elo/Glicko) and series-format win probability
mlb.mlbb_team_rating_series_format.mechanism: Match win probability depends on team strength and the best-of format that compresses or amplifies the gap.
mlb.mlbb_team_rating_series_format.rationale: KXMLBBGAME is not baseball; the relevant information is esports team strength, recent roster and patch changes, and map-level results (draft pick and ban), series length (best-of-3 or 5), and regional context.
mlb.mlbb_team_rating_series_format.measurement: Glicko-2 rating per team from map-level results (last 12 months, rating deviation decay), roster-change penalty (reset 30% of rating if >=2 starters change), patch-change variance inflation; match win probability from per-game win probability p and series format: best-of-3 P = p^2(3-2p), best-of-5 P = sum. As-of: at roster lock before the match. Units: probability.
raw_data: match-level: teams, map results, drafts, roster, patch, date
mlb.mlbb_team_rating_series_format.why: Provides the only relevant information for the esports contract and keeps baseball features from contaminating it.

interactions.mechanism: Award probability rises with wins over expectation but saturates once a candidate is clearly the leading narrative; additional wins add less, while a competing candidate with a division title can flip the ordering. News about finalists is the information event that resets the field.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit multinomial logit on historical finalist votes with candidate score and test saturation in the score term.

interactions.mechanism: Completion before the deadline is nearly impossible before a signed agreement and highly probable after the owners' vote is scheduled; the relationship between time remaining and probability is a threshold that depends on stage, so the same news at different stages has different value.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate stage-specific completion probability and duration; test time-remaining x stage interaction.

interactions.mechanism: Series format compresses strength gaps: a best-of-5 favours the stronger team more than a best-of-3 at the same per-game probability, and refund rules for postponement and forfeits remove a small mass; the rating gap maps concavely to match probability.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare calibration of ratings-based match probabilities by series format.

interactions.mechanism: Reports precede official announcements, but the rules count only the official event (for sale: finalization and league approval), so the value of a report depends on its source credibility and on how far the process still has to run; price reaction is evaluated against what the rules will count.
interactions.how_to_test: Score historical reports by outcome and measure lead time between report and official announcement.

interactions.mechanism: Hazards of hiring and sale news concentrate around calendar anchors (season end, winter meetings, league meetings), so time-conditioned base rates are piecewise in the calendar; the market window relative to these anchors drives probability.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate calendar-dependent hazard from past years and compare with constant-hazard model.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating logistic in score with a threshold for division title
nonlinearities.why: Award votes concentrate on one or two candidates, so probability rises steeply near the top and flattens beyond a clear lead.

nonlinearities.shape: Step-like by stage with right-skewed durations
nonlinearities.why: Probability of closing before a date jumps at signing and again at the owners' vote, with long and uncertain delays between.

nonlinearities.shape: S-shaped: match win probability steepens with rating gap and series length
nonlinearities.why: Best-of formats amplify the better team's edge nonlinearly, so a fixed rating gap converts to different match probabilities in best-of-3 and best-of-5.

nonlinearities.shape: Time-varying hazard: nonuniform across the market window
nonlinearities.why: Events cluster around calendar dates; a uniform hazard would misprice early and late windows.

contract.settlement_definition: Mixed participation family. KXMLBSTART pays Yes if the named player is in the official starting batting order (including as designated hitter) when the game begins; announcement in an earlier lineup then replacement before the game begins resolves No, and entering later as a pinch hitter or substitute does not qualify. KXMLBPITCH pays Yes if the named player records at least one pitch in a regular-season game inside a date window (example after Jul 28 and before Sep 28, 2026). KXMLBNEXTTEAM (filed here but a transaction market) pays for the team the player is with or signs with by a date, with a Retires/No Team strike. KXMLBSTARTER, KXMLBSTARTINGLINEUP and KXMLBDEBUT are title-only.

rules_evidence.quote: Resolution is based on the official starting batting order recorded by the governing league.
rules_evidence.establishes: Start market settles on the official starting batting order at game start (including DH), not on a probable or announced lineup.

rules_evidence.quote: Entering the game later as a pinch hitter or other substitute does not qualify.
rules_evidence.establishes: Substitutes do not count, so the market is a pure starting-lineup event.

rules_evidence.quote: must record at least 1 pitch in a Pro Baseball regular season game after Jul 28, 2026 and before Sep 28, 2026
rules_evidence.establishes: Pitch-in-window market is a multi-game availability event (regular season only) with a date window, not a single-game start.

rules_evidence.quote: If Ronald Acuna is a free agent, whether restricted or unrestricted, for any period of time and signs a contract with any team, including their previous team, the market for that team will resolve Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: Next-team market is a free-agent/trade transaction outcome, mechanically a transaction market misfiled under participation.

variants_and_edge_cases: Population differs: a single-game starting lineup market, a window-long 'will he pitch' market and a next-team transaction market have different hazards (managerial decision, injury/rehab progression, free-agent signing).

Start market: an announced lineup that changes before first pitch resolves No (late scratch), so lineup posting time and warm-up scratch hazard matter; a player who starts as pitcher qualifies only if he is in the batting order.

Pitch window: regular season only (postseason pitches do not count in the sampled text), 'after' and 'before' dates are exclusive, and rehab appearances in the minors presumably do not count; exact handling of injury list is not stated.

Next-team: extension or re-signing with the same team does not trigger early resolution; a player who remains on his team at the date resolves for that team; retirement or no contract resolves the Retires/No Team strike.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official starting batting order recorded by the league (MLB Stats API game feed) for start markets; league game logs for pitch counts; transaction records for next team.

mechanism.summary: Participation contracts depend on a manager's decision conditional on a player's availability. For a single game the chain is: roster status (active, injured list, minors), the manager's rest and platoon policy for that day (day game after night game, catcher rest, opposing starter handedness, DH rotation), posting of the lineup card a few hours before first pitch, and the residual chance of a late scratch between posting and the first pitch. Before the card posts the probability is a mixture over the manager's patterns, after it is near one unless the player is hurt in warm-up. For windows (will he pitch between two dates) availability is a hazard process: a returning player must progress through a rehab sequence, the team must have a role and a reason (race, rest of rotation), and injury risk can end it. For next-team markets the object is a free-agency or trade transaction. The edge lies in knowing the timing of information (lineup posting relative to price) and in the specific manager and player, not in team strength.

stages.name: Roster status and health gate
stages.description: A player must be on the active roster and healthy; IL placement, minor-league assignment, rehab status and day-to-day injuries set the upper bound on the probability of any participation. Injury information arrives through official transactions and beat reports and is timestamped, so the information vintage determines the model state.
stages.distribution: Mostly 0/1 with an uncertain middle for day-to-day and returning players.

stages.name: Manager's decision for the specific game
stages.description: Given health, the manager decides to start the player based on role (everyday, platoon, bench), the opposing starter's handedness, rest patterns after travel or a night game, catcher and veteran rest conventions, DH rotation and lineup construction style, and in September or when clinched, rest and prospect-call-up policy. Players on a platoon sit against same-handed starters unless exceptions apply.
stages.distribution: Binary, with probabilities of start by role: everyday about 0.9, platoon 0.3-0.7 by opposing hand, bench near 0.1.

stages.name: Lineup posting and late-scratch hazard
stages.description: The lineup card is posted several hours before first pitch; the start market is effectively resolved then, except for the late-scratch hazard between posting and the first pitch (pregame injury, illness, warm-up). The market contract resolves No if the announced lineup changes before the game, so the late-scratch probability conditional on posting is a small but non-zero residual that depends on the player's injury status.
stages.distribution: Time-to-event: near-certain at card posting; residual probability of a scratch about 1-3% for listed starters, higher with day-to-day injuries.

stages.name: Window availability and exposure
stages.description: The pitch-in-window market integrates over games: the probability that a player records at least one pitch in a window is one minus the product of per-game non-appearance probabilities, but failures are strongly correlated through an absorbing injury state and through the team's plan, so a hazard model with injury absorption is appropriate. A rehabbing or two-way player needs a plan for pitching.
stages.distribution: Compound survival with absorption; per-game probabilities correlated; right-censored by season end.

stages.name: Transaction-type outcomes in the archetype
stages.description: The next-team and debut markets in this archetype depend on contract status and free-agency or trade behaviour rather than a manager's lineup choices; they share only the label 'player move'. They should be modelled in the transactions archetype with contract and market inputs.
stages.distribution: Heavy-tailed time-to-event distribution with seasonality.

officiating_rules.note: No officiating factor affects whether a player starts; only roster rules (active roster size, option and IL rules) matter, which are captured in settlement and roster-move inputs.

mlb.late_scratch_hazard.label: Late-scratch hazard between lineup posting and first pitch (conditional on listed starter)
mlb.late_scratch_hazard.mechanism: A posted lineup can still change before the game for illness, injury or warm-up discomfort.
mlb.late_scratch_hazard.rationale: KXMLBSTART resolves No if the player is announced in a lineup and replaced before the game begins; the probability is low on average but elevated for players with day-to-day injuries and for catchers and pitchers.
mlb.late_scratch_hazard.measurement: Over 4 seasons of posted lineups and official starting orders compute P(listed starter not in final starting order) by player injury flag (none, day-to-day, recently returned), position and time between posting and first pitch; logistic with random effect per team (communication practice) shrunk k = 100 games. Output hazard per player-game. As-of: at the lineup posting timestamp. Units: probability.
free_sources: MLB Stats API lineup changes (historical vintage unverified)
raw_data: lineup snapshots by timestamp, final starting order, injury flags
mlb.late_scratch_hazard.why: The contract's No-on-replacement rule makes this hazard a term in the price after the card posts.

mlb.rehab_progression_stage.label: Rehab progression stage and return-to-pitch/play timeline for injured players
mlb.rehab_progression_stage.mechanism: A returning player must progress through defined rehab steps before appearing, so timing depends on the stage reached.
mlb.rehab_progression_stage.rationale: Window markets such as 'will he pitch before a date' are hazard problems; the information is the rehab stage (throwing program, bullpen sessions, simulated games, minor-league rehab assignment) and the team's stated timetable.
mlb.rehab_progression_stage.measurement: Map each injured player to stages (0 no throwing, 1 long toss, 2 bullpens, 3 simulated/live batting practice, 4 rehab games, 5 activated). Historical stage-to-activation durations by injury type (shoulder, elbow, hamstring) from IL transaction records and rehab-assignment logs; fit survival (Weibull) per injury class with player-age covariates and shrinkage k = 10 players per class. P(pitch in window) = P(activation before window end) x P(used in a game in window | activated). As-of: latest stage report. Units: probability.
raw_data: transactions with dates, rehab assignments by date, injury type, stage reports
mlb.rehab_progression_stage.why: KXMLBPITCH and similar windows depend on rehab timing rather than games played.

mlb.window_exposure_schedule.label: Window exposure: games, off days, doubleheaders and role-probability per game within the window
mlb.window_exposure_schedule.mechanism: A multi-game window aggregates per-game participation probabilities with schedule structure.
mlb.window_exposure_schedule.rationale: P(at least one) in a window depends on the number of team games remaining (off days, doubleheaders, postponement) and on the team's usage pattern; a two-way player's pitching is limited by rotation turns.
mlb.window_exposure_schedule.measurement: N = count of team regular-season games in the window (from schedule; subtract postponements risk). Per-game p_g from the single-game model with rotation slot (for pitchers: number of rotation turns = N/5 rounded). P(at least one) = 1 - Prod(1 - p_g x P(healthy through g)) with injury hazard h per game from injuries_pit. Include end-of-season rest and clinched policy. Units: probability. As-of: daily.
raw_data: schedule with dates, rotation order, off days
mlb.window_exposure_schedule.why: Converts single-game probabilities to window-level probability with correct correlation structure.

interactions.mechanism: A platoon player sits against same-handed starters and rests after night games, so start probability is a conditional product of role, opposing hand and rest pattern; for everyday players only the rest pattern matters, so the effect of handedness is gated by role.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit start logistic with role x hand x rest-day terms and compare calibration by role.

interactions.mechanism: Before the card posts the probability is a mixture of manager patterns, after posting it collapses to the scratch hazard; the transition is a step in time at posting, so the value of information is concentrated at posting relative to market close.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare model error before and after the observed posting timestamp for historical games.

interactions.mechanism: Window availability is a survival process: rehab stage determines time to activation, injury hazard after activation determines early failure, and the number of games available determines how many opportunities there are; failures across games are correlated through the absorbing state.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate window-level probability with and without correlated absorption; compare to naive product of per-game probabilities.

interactions.mechanism: After a team clinches a seed or is eliminated, rest probability switches regime: regulars sit and prospects play, with the size of the switch depending on the manager's style and on whether seeding still matters; before clinching the baseline pattern applies.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate start probability by standings state (clinched/eliminated) and manager; test the discontinuity at clinching date.

interactions.mechanism: Role changes (call-up, trade, injury replacement) announced by news shift start probability at a discrete date, so the window model must restart its per-game probabilities at the change; the number of games after the change drives the window probability.
interactions.how_to_test: Segment games by role-change date and compare window predictions with piecewise versus constant role probabilities.

nonlinearities.shape: Small base rate with threshold increase for day-to-day injuries
nonlinearities.why: Probability is near zero for healthy players and rises sharply with a recorded day-to-day designation, so a linear effect misses the regime.

nonlinearities.shape: Step function by stage with right-skewed durations
nonlinearities.why: Progress through rehab stages is discrete and the time to the next stage is skewed by setbacks, so timing is not smooth in elapsed days.

nonlinearities.shape: Concave in number of games: 1 - prod(1 - p) saturates with exposure
nonlinearities.why: With many games available, additional games add little to P(at least one); with few games, each adds a lot.

nonlinearities.shape: Regime step at clinching or elimination date
nonlinearities.why: Rest policy changes discontinuously at the point stakes disappear.

contract.settlement_definition: No live series is classified under this archetype; the transaction-type markets trade as KXMLBNEXTTEAM (next team before a date, with Retires/No Team) in the participation bucket and KXMLBCOACH (next manager) in the off-field bucket (title only). The sampled NEXTTEAM rule pays Yes for the team the player is with or signs a contract with by the date, counts a free agent signing with any team including the previous one, and does not treat an extension with the same team as an early resolution; retirement or no signing resolves the Retires/No Team strike. Manager and trade markets rely on official announcement but their rules are not sampled.
variants_and_edge_cases: Next-team: a player who stays with his team resolves Yes for that team at the date, a free agent who signs elsewhere resolves for the new team; extensions while under contract do not resolve early.

Official announcement versus reports: contracts typically require the official transaction (announced signing or trade completed), so a reported agreement subject to a physical exam does not resolve until official; medical failure can void.
Manager markets: the next manager of a team requires a hire announcement, and interim managers are an edge case not covered in the sample.
Deadline structure: trade-deadline, non-tender, qualifying offer and Rule 5 dates create calendar clusters where the market window includes or excludes them.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official team or league transaction announcements (MLB transactions log); not named in the sibling rules.

mechanism.summary: Transactions follow institutional calendars and incentives, so the event is a time-to-event process with hazards that change by date and context. For trades, a seller with a short-contract player is likely to deal near the deadline and the buyer-seller status of the team is driven by playoff probability and payroll; for free-agent signings, contract expiry, qualifying-offer decisions, positional market and team payroll space drive timing, with most signings clustered in the first weeks of free agency and again at the winter meetings; for manager changes, tenure, team underperformance relative to expectations, owner statements and contract status matter. Beat-writer reports precede most official moves, with source credibility varying; the contract resolves on the official announcement, so lead times and process failures (physicals, vetoes) matter. There is little statistical structure in team performance beyond its effect on incentives, so the best-supported approach is reference-class hazard modelling updated by timestamped reports.

stages.name: Eligibility and constraints
stages.description: A transaction requires that the player or manager is eligible: contract expiry or opt-out for free agency, service time and 40-man status for call-ups and trades, no-trade protections and 10-and-5 rights, club options, and the qualifying offer system. The constraint set determines which events are possible at all and when.
stages.distribution: Binary feasibility gating with time-varying eligibility dates.

stages.name: Team incentives and finances
stages.description: Buyer or seller status depends on playoff probability and distance to contention; payroll and luxury-tax thresholds constrain the ability to add salary; managers are fired when expectations are missed and the organization is willing to pay a replacement. Incentives are partly observable from standings and projections.
stages.distribution: Continuous incentive index with threshold behaviour at playoff-odds boundaries.

stages.name: Calendar and process timing
stages.description: Transaction hazards are not constant: trade deadline day, the end-of-season window, the non-tender and qualifying-offer deadlines, the winter meetings, the Rule 5 draft and the start of spring training concentrate events on known dates. Process steps (negotiation, physical, league review) add lags between agreement and official announcement.
stages.distribution: Piecewise-constant hazard with spikes at calendar anchors; lag distribution from agreement to official.

stages.name: Information flow and report credibility
stages.description: Credible reporters often announce agreements hours or days before official announcements; the probability of eventual official completion given a report depends on the report's wording ('close to', 'agreed', 'pending physical') and on the reporter's track record. Prices respond to reports, so the quantity of interest is the posterior given report text and source.
stages.distribution: Bayesian update with source-specific likelihood ratios; most information arrives in discrete jumps.

stages.name: Resolution wording and failure modes
stages.description: Contracts resolve on an official announcement meeting specified conditions; failures include a physical that voids a deal, a veto, a change of mind or a rule specifying a different team (sign-and-trade). The market window may also close before an announced deal becomes official.
stages.distribution: Absorbing event with small failure mass after report; wording determines edge cases.

role_personnel.note: Contract and eligibility of the player.

opponent_matchup.note: Transactions have no head-to-head matchup; a rival team's competition for a free agent is a market-structure factor handled through payroll headroom and calendar, not a matchup variable.

environment.note: Venue, weather and altitude do not affect transaction timing; location of a team may affect free agent preferences only weakly and is not measurable in a way a market can price.

pace_volume.note: There is no volume of opportunities in a transaction event; the quantity analogous to pace is the calendar hazard rate, included under calendar timing.

efficiency_conversion.note: No conversion rate per opportunity applies; the nearest object is the stage conversion from report to official announcement, included as report credibility.

officiating_rules.note: Roster and transaction rules (CBA windows, Rule 5, option rules) matter and are included in service time and eligibility inputs; there are no officials whose tendencies matter.

mlb.contract_status_and_service_clock.label: Contract status and service clock (expiry, options, opt-outs, no-trade, qualifying-offer eligibility)
mlb.contract_status_and_service_clock.mechanism: Transactions are possible only when contractual and CBA conditions allow them.
mlb.contract_status_and_service_clock.rationale: A player's free-agency status, club or player option, no-trade protection, arbitration status and service time determine the set and timing of feasible events; 'next team' markets differ sharply for players under contract versus free agents.
mlb.contract_status_and_service_clock.measurement: Per player: contract end year, options (club/player/mutual with decision dates), opt-out dates, no-trade clause, 10-5 rights, arbitration years, qualifying-offer eligibility (service with one team, prior QO), service-time days at date. Output eligibility flags and dates. As-of: latest public contract data. Units: flags and dates.
raw_data: player contract table: years, options, clauses, service time
mlb.contract_status_and_service_clock.why: Defines feasibility and timing, which are first-order for next-team markets.

mlb.news_source_reliability_score.label: Source-level reliability: P(official | report type) from historical reports
mlb.news_source_reliability_score.mechanism: Not all reports are equal; some reporters' 'agreement reached' items are nearly always followed by official moves.
mlb.news_source_reliability_score.rationale: Market reaction to reports is only warranted if the posterior given the source and wording exceeds the market's pricing; track record and wording ('close', 'agreed', 'pending physical') strongly change completion probability.
mlb.news_source_reliability_score.measurement: For each reporter-source and wording class compute historical fraction of reports that led to the official event within 14 days (Beta posterior with prior from class average, k = 10 reports) and distribution of lead time. Output P(official by date) and expected lead. As-of: report timestamp. Units: probability and days.
free_sources: social media archives (unavailable_public via API limits)
raw_data: report-level: source, text, timestamp, outcome and official date
mlb.news_source_reliability_score.why: Provides the likelihood ratio for the most important information type.

mlb.calendar_hazard_by_event_type.label: Calendar hazard function by transaction type (trade, free-agent signing, extension, manager hire)
mlb.calendar_hazard_by_event_type.mechanism: Hazard of each event type is concentrated on known dates.
mlb.calendar_hazard_by_event_type.rationale: Using a flat per-day rate misprices markets that straddle deadlines and meeting dates; for example, a large share of free-agent signings occur in specific off-season windows and trade completions spike near the deadline.
mlb.calendar_hazard_by_event_type.measurement: From 15 years of transactions: daily event counts per type normalized by eligible stock; fit a piecewise log-linear hazard with calendar-anchor dummies (deadline week, winter meetings week, non-tender day, spring training start). Output h(d) for the window dates and survival to the end. Shrink per-type to pooled with k = 3 seasons. Units: events per eligible per day. As-of: current stock of eligible players.
raw_data: transactions with dates and types; eligible-stock counts
mlb.calendar_hazard_by_event_type.why: Gives time-conditioned base rates instead of one reference-class rate.

mlb.cbt_payroll_headroom.label: Competitive-balance-tax and payroll headroom for the acquiring team
mlb.cbt_payroll_headroom.mechanism: Finance constrains who can absorb salary.
mlb.cbt_payroll_headroom.rationale: Teams near luxury-tax thresholds or with stated payroll limits are much less likely to add salary; headroom also determines trade behaviour.
mlb.cbt_payroll_headroom.measurement: Headroom = CBT threshold - projected CBT payroll (average annual value of contracts for 40-man roster + benefits) for the team at the date; flags for crossing the first/second threshold; share of owner-stated budget. Units: dollars and flag. As-of: latest transaction.
raw_data: team payroll table, thresholds
mlb.cbt_payroll_headroom.why: Explains who can sign or trade for salary and so conditions signing and trade probabilities.

mlb.manager_firing_hazard.label: Manager seat heat: tenure, underperformance vs expectation, contract expiry and owner statements
mlb.manager_firing_hazard.mechanism: Managers are removed when results fall short of expectations and the owner or front office is willing to act.
mlb.manager_firing_hazard.rationale: Next-manager markets resolve on a hiring event preceded by a vacancy; the vacancy hazard depends on wins below projection, contract status, front-office change and public statements.
mlb.manager_firing_hazard.measurement: Hazard = logistic on (wins - preseason projected wins) per 162, tenure years, contract years remaining (<=1 flag), prior-year playoff flag, recent front-office change, and winning percentage trailing 30 games; calibrate on 20 years of mid-season and off-season manager changes (shrink k = 3 seasons). Units: probability of vacancy before date. As-of: current day.
raw_data: manager-season table: team results, contract status, change events
mlb.manager_firing_hazard.why: The vacancy hazard is the first stage of next-manager contracts.

mlb.roster_moves.reason: Transaction log is the ground truth feed; as a raw feed it is not a driver without hazard modelling.

mlb.seller_buyer_status.reason: Buyer/seller incentives drive trades and call-ups; derived from playoff odds and need explicit thresholds.

mlb.service_time_rules.reason: Option, 40-man and Rule 5 constraints define feasibility windows; partially covered by contract status.

mlb.news.reason: Reports precede official moves; value depends on source credibility.

mlb.injuries_pit.reason: Injuries trigger IL moves and call-ups and shape trade behaviour.

mlb.season_sim.reason: Playoff odds define buyer/seller status; this duplicates seller_buyer_status in use but supplies the quantity.

mlb.offfield_base_rate.reason: One reference class for heterogeneous events is inadequate; a time-conditioned hazard per event type is needed.

m.rules_text.reason: What counts as official and how extensions and sign-and-trades are handled determine the event.

m.quote_history.reason: Price reaction to reports is a market response, only useful to evaluate report credibility.

interactions.mechanism: A seller with an expiring contract in the final weeks before the deadline has a trade hazard that is the product of team status (seller), player contract (expiring, tradable) and calendar proximity, so none of these alone predicts a trade; each multiplies the daily hazard.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit Cox hazard with interaction of seller status, expiring contract and days to deadline.

interactions.mechanism: The completion probability given a report depends on wording and source, and on whether the rules count only the official announcement; a credible 'pending physical' report implies high probability of completion within days but not certainty.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate completion probability by source-wording class and time since report.

interactions.mechanism: Payroll headroom acts as a threshold: teams near the tax line are very unlikely to add salary beyond it, so a free-agent signing probability for that team is near zero until headroom exceeds the contract's annual value; contract structure shifts the effective threshold.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate signing probability by headroom to AAV ratio and test discontinuity near zero headroom.

interactions.mechanism: Managers are fired in-season mainly when the team is out of contention, and in the offseason after the season ends; the hazard regime switches at the end of the season, and the next-manager market depends on a vacancy created in the first regime or second.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate hazard in regular season versus offseason and test dependence on playoff odds.

interactions.mechanism: Injury-driven call-ups and IL moves are constrained by roster and option rules, so the number of available call-up slots and the date relative to roster expansions changes the hazard in steps.
interactions.how_to_test: Segment history by roster-rule regime and compare call-up rates.

nonlinearities.shape: Piecewise-constant spikes at calendar anchors
nonlinearities.why: Events cluster around fixed dates, so cumulative probability over a window is a step-like function of window placement.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold at playoff odds about 10-20% where teams flip from buyers to sellers
nonlinearities.why: Teams behave discontinuously around the contention boundary, so a linear function of playoff odds misprices behaviour.

nonlinearities.shape: Beta-posterior shrinkage with source report count
nonlinearities.why: Reliability is estimated from few reports per source, so posterior probability depends nonlinearly on counts.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold at zero headroom
nonlinearities.why: Teams avoid crossing tax lines, so signing probability collapses near and below zero headroom.
